The question was drafted live. The facilitator put 'How do we cultivate a culture of sustainability and reciprocity within our communities?' to the circle twice, a participant proposed swapping reciprocity for peaceful coexistence with nature, and the facilitator then proposed trimming to peaceful coexistence alone on the ground that it already contains sustainability. That drew agreement but was never restated as a whole sentence, so the archived wording is the agreed trim, assembled from two voices rather than spoken by one.

theories.text: Venus as the result of unchecked global warming, and a possible future for Earth.
The politics of being over having: economic growth is measured as having more.
Denial avoids uncomfortable truths; the discomfort must be felt before anything is done.
Other beings may feel; their language is simply unintelligible to humans.
Strike the word resources: what is taken is taken because it is needed.
Individual actions are necessary, but the levers over mass-scale waste sit elsewhere.
People do whatever is most important to them at that moment in time.
Altruism is not the ask; reciprocity between people and the natural world is.
Two concepts named: an economic incentive, and a cultural incentive tied to identity.
Change at the bay happens at the grassroots level, not through experts alone.
Education that makes people feel bad is blocked out rather than heard.
Time in nature revives enjoyment, and enjoyment becomes the choice to protect it.
Every durable success translated the environmental ask into the decider's own immediate interest.
One or two children per class carry the change; broad interest is unnecessary.
A stable environment is business infrastructure; the benefit loops back to the firm.
No individual hero solves this; accumulated small acts become a movement.
Calling the world resources turns stewardship into a competition over who owns what.

applications.text: Chesapeake Bay Foundation - farmers persuaded to grow riparian buffer zones between fields and creeks.
Clean the bay days - public agencies release employees to clean the bay during the workday.
Japan - Itadakimasu gives gratitude for the whole chain of sacrifice behind a meal.
Paris Olympics - a city river cleaned up for the Games, named in the room as the Rhine.
Gulf Coast United States - chemical plants sited in predominantly African American neighborhoods.
Residents of those neighborhoods pushed back at grassroots level and raised the awareness themselves.
Greta Thunberg - left school to sit at Sweden's legislature and drew others into activism.
Canada - two school days a year with no formal lessons, children roaming and playing.
Neighborhood patches - neighborhoods take responsibility for maintaining a portion of the growth around them.
A local beekeeping club - a volunteer organizer teaches non-beekeepers why pollinators matter.
School beekeeping clubs, and a public observation hive maintained in return for club space.

sources.text: Indigenous wisdom belongs in environmental policy discussions at every level.
David Suzuki Foundation - indigenous wisdom applied at scale across science, policy, and community.
Chesapeake Bay Foundation's large outreach as the route to community involvement.
Commands, businesses, and boys and girls clubs recruited as partner groups.
Schools already holding classes outdoors in local parks, as partners for community projects.
A local volunteer organiser to be invited into a future forum.
Nuts-and-bolts process detail wanted from a grassroots organiser, not anecdote.
Article on the Venus-to-Earth comparison, sent to the group from astronomy.com.
Article on chemical plants along the Gulf Coast, to be found and shared.
The endeavor website offered as reference on making time for the next generation.
Businesses to create space for employees to cultivate a relationship with nature.
Government policy to supply the tools, resources, money, and incentives.
Merlin - an app that identifies birds by their song, raised through a school.
Shinrin-yoku forest therapy - national policy led by Japan's fisheries and forest ministry.
A participant's podcast, already carrying an interview with a sustainability practitioner.
Library books in Canada on young environmental activists, as material for children.
Storyboards from previous inquiries available on request to anyone curious.
A real-time storyboard format still being sought; current storyboards are snapshots.
Technical improvements and suggestions invited from the forum for future iterations.
A need for transparency on how environmental funding is spent and whether it worked.
A need for indigenous governance seated where building and resource priorities are decided.
Time is the scarce input; without hours carved out, every entry point stays unused.
Documented successes are the missing input; the circle could name mostly failures.
This inquiry enters at community and local-government level, skipping the personal one.
The record itself needs distributing: summaries sent on, storyboards republished, updates visible between gatherings.

policies.text: Discourse must lead to tangible change; accountability and personal responsibility are stated norms.
Riparian buffer policy - grants for the work, or tax benefit for surrendering 100 feet of creek bank.
Policy sets funding and executive priority, leaving states and provinces fighting for federal funding.
Facilitator proposed peaceful coexistence alone; the archived question matches that trim, unrestated.
Agencies grant excused workday absence for bay clean-ups, signaling institutional stewardship.
Throwing ships' trash overboard, once tolerated, now carries jail time.
India legislated natural rights for the Ganges River; corruption claims and opaque spending stalled it.
Shinrin-yoku - national forest therapy policy from Japan's fisheries and forestry ministry after 1980s overwork.
Singapore builds sustainability into national identity because land and space are scarce.
Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission addresses injustice against First Nations, Inuit, and Metis.
Truth and reconciliation policy acknowledges a need for indigenous governance in resource decisions.
The Endeavor - a globally minded organization carrying wisdom from one country to another.
The vote is the available lever where profit is weighed against what is lost.
Reputation, once at stake, converts tolerated harm into policed prohibition.

opportunities.text: A positive spin on the warning invites action rather than resignation.
Emptied lockdown roads cleared Los Angeles smog, proof that change shows fast.
Grants or a tax benefit make surrendering creek margins worthwhile for farmers.
Employers release staff during the workday for cleanups as an excused absence.
Cleanup is good politics: oystermen, fishermen and watermen vote and remember.
Commands, businesses and youth clubs are ready channels for grassroots recruitment.
Open school days without formal lessons could carry community garden projects.
Teaching people who will never keep bees to spare pollinators sets a reachable ask.
Local schools took up beekeeping clubs after one organiser's sustained outreach.
The Merlin app identifies birds by song, and knowing species builds care.
Indirect encouragement teaches environmental care better than telling people directly.
Once the connection to nature is personal, people advocate for it themselves.
Talking about the cause at every chance produces encounters with people who can amplify it.
Wisdom from those who already walked the path beats research from books.
Governments already invite indigenous input into how to build and prioritize resources.
A local volunteer organiser may be invited to a coming gathering.
The community grant proposal includes forest bathing as space for healing.
Aristotle's Lyceum let people come and go, so guests need not stay.
Storyboards are snapshots; live-updating formats are being explored for newcomers.
Late joiners are greeted in the chat and absorbed without pausing discussion.

challenges.text: Warming likened to a frog in boiling water, with some people already burned.
Media that instills fear paralyzes people instead of moving them to act.
Clear skies during lockdown were forgotten as soon as traffic and smog returned.
People with no felt connection to a watershed have no reason to protect it.
Governments place the onus on individuals, then push it onto the next generation.
India's attempt to legislate rights for a sacred river met corruption and ineffective governance.
Chemical plants along the Gulf Coast left Black neighborhoods with elevated cancer rates.
Grassroots pushback against industry may take three generations to show results.
Global examples of failing to protect nature outnumber the successes.
Indigenous stewardship wisdom was lost in the race for industry and progress.
Swaying large corporations and governments stays difficult even for effective foundations.
Multiple jobs and shuttling children leave no time to build a relationship with nature.
Competition for resources is ingrained in Western thinking as the law of the jungle.
Communities already convinced of one way are an uphill climb to influence.
Greta Thunberg's activism is dismissed as a child who knows nothing.
Several invited people could not attend, citing busy schedules.
Media shows the event and never the years of build-up that produced it.

inquiries.quote: the 1st step is to make it important for them. Why would a guy who maybe doesn't have a connection to the bay care about the bay? You got to draw that connection to him.
inquiries.callToAction: The inquiry was taken on as a personal responsibility rather than left with the circle. One participant undertook to speak within the week with a local volunteer organiser, to bring back the practical processes behind that grassroots outreach rather than anecdotes, and to report next month on the conversation and on their own volunteering. The same participant undertook to ask whether that organiser would join a later forum for a short visit rather than a whole session, an idea the circle endorsed and the facilitator welcomed on the precedent that Aristotle's Lyceum let people come and go. The facilitator volunteered to carry the inquiry alongside that participant so it would not rest on one person, and undertook to send the written inquiry summary to a participant attending for the first time. Two participants are jointly preparing a community grant application to run this forum as a monthly live event in a Vancouver neighborhood facing poverty, with forest bathing written in as the healing element, and the processes learned from grassroots organizing are to shape that project. One participant undertook to find and circulate the articles behind the evening's opening example and the Gulf Coast case. Work on the previous inquiry, into mentoring adolescents to adulthood, continues toward an updated storyboard: one participant reported early-phase research and reading, and one further steward, withheld, holds that call to action with them. The facilitator undertook to supply the editable storyboard format to both, then republish it and resend it to the group.

storyboard.logline: Five voices across North America, joined silently by a sixth, turned a magazine article about Venus into a question about how a community lives with nature rather than off it.
storyboard.arcNotes: The evening ran the standard sequence and stayed unusually close to one thread: an article comparing Venus with Earth was offered in the first minute of open discussion, and every later section circled the same mechanism - people, farmers, employers, agencies and governments act on what has been made important to them at the moment they decide, and the natural world benefits as a byproduct rather than as a motive. The theories section produced two named incentives, economic and cultural. The application section produced more failures than successes: a stalled attempt to give a sacred river legal standing, chemical plants sited in neighbourhoods that had to organise before anyone listened, and one durable success in a watershed foundation that pays farmers to keep cattle out of creeks. The turn inward came late, through sources and inputs, where the answers stopped being institutions and became children planting seagrass, open school days, a beekeeping club, a bird-song app and forest therapy - small entry points that give a person a relationship worth defending. Convergence was practical: one participant took the inquiry as a personal responsibility with a report due the following month, and the facilitator tied it to a grant application that would put this forum into a live monthly event in a part of one city that needs hope. The closing circle was brief, grateful, and produced the evening's clearest sign of movement, a stated change of mind about bees. QUESTION, DISPUTED - the archive should not stand as it is. It records the inquiry as "How do we cultivate peaceful co-existence with nature within our communities?". No such sentence is spoken. The facilitator's first draft, assembled live on the screen, was a respect for nature within our communities (@30:07 to @30:28). After the policy and reciprocity discussion the facilitator twice put a revised wording to the group for agreement, contiguous both times: "how do we cultivate a culture of sustainability and reciprocity within our communities" (@37:29) and "How do we cultivate a culture of sustainability and reciprocity within our communities?" (@37:58). The peaceful coexistence form came from a different participant moments later (@38:47 to @38:53), spread across three cues, pairing peaceful coexistence with nature with a culture of sustainability and saying "in our communities" rather than "within". The facilitator's reply was "Or perhaps just the peaceful coexistence, because, you know, that could include sustainability." (@38:57), which drew agreement, but no finished sentence is restated before the recording ends at @1:28:10. The archived string is therefore a composite of two speakers that also drops the culture of sustainability the facilitator had explicitly retained. Two defensible fixes: record the facilitator's verbatim wording, or keep the composite and mark it as agreed in the room and assembled from two voices. Leaving it unmarked is not one of them.

beats.title: Opening, norms, and five breaths
beats.summary: The facilitator opened for the two hosts, framed the evening as an hour and a half of meaningful discussion meant to strengthen bonds of friendship and fellowship around issues that affect the local community, and ran the reminders: an online forum, now drawing from across North America, held to the golden rule, everyone in it a peer, looking for commonalities while acknowledging differences with respect. The agenda was walked through - opening of presence, a recap of the September inquiry, shared understanding, the sequence of inquiry, administrative highlights, and a closing fellowship circle for gratitude. A new joiner who did not speak was asked to confirm by chat that the audio was working; the chat's first line was a thumbs-up reaction and a one-word welcome followed (chat clock 00:22:27 and 00:22:48, recording @1:30 and @1:51). The opening of presence was offered as five breaths, a practice credited in the room to an indigenous tribe in Hawaii, each inhale and pause carrying one intention: gratitude to the earth, to ancestors, to oneself, to family and friends, and to the children whose choices the work is for.
beats.pullQuote: the planet that sustains all life, both the human world and the natural world
beats.slideHint: Title slide for the Lyceum as an endeavor for families and communities, a rules and norms panel with the five Ws (about ninety minutes, online forum, North America, golden rule, peers, commonality and difference), the agenda strip, and an Opening of Presence slide listing the five breath intentions in order.

beats.title: Recap: mentoring adolescents to adulthood
beats.summary: The floor went to the participant who had volunteered to carry the September inquiry forward - how to mentor adolescents to adulthood - jointly with one further steward, withheld. The update placed the work in an early research and data collection phase with several options open. A recent tour given to young people who were weighing up a career path, or had just committed to one, had been used to talk about more than the work itself: life lessons, career paths forward, and an early job as a stepping stone to whatever comes after, with the knowledge carried on into later opportunities. Books had been read and notes taken, and the two stewards were to compile the material into an addition to the storyboard and a more concrete way ahead on how mentorship programmes bring mentors and young people together. The facilitator answered that storyboards are snapshots in time, that the group is exploring formats that show updates as they happen so a later reader does not begin from a static document, and that the editable file would go to both stewards and be republished to the group.
beats.pullQuote: These storyboards are just snapshots in time
beats.slideHint: Recap slide for the September inquiry, 'How do we mentor adolescents to adulthood?', with status marked early research and data collection, the steward line reading one steward plus one withheld, and a callout that the storyboard is a living document republished after each update.

beats.title: Shared understanding
beats.summary: Four voices introduced themselves against prompts for cultural background, family composition and connection to the Lyceum, the facilitator noting that the previous circle had been four or five people and that the practice exists so peers can know who is who. What the round established is recorded here at the level of the circle rather than person by person. The heritages named across it reached from North America and Latin America to Europe, the Middle East and East Asia, more than one person carrying several at once, so the room held considerably more ancestry than a count of five would suggest. Most of the connections to the forum predated it: this was largely a circle of people who already knew one another rather than strangers assembled for the evening. The reason given for being in the room was consistent across the round - an interest in bettering humanity and in reaching out from the family to the local level. The endeavor itself was traced to long phone conversations about mentorship a year and a half to two years earlier.
beats.pullQuote: I'm continuing to look at bettering the humanity and reaching out from our families to the local level

beats.title: Seeing the circle globally
beats.summary: Two maps set the frame before the inquiry opened. A United Nations world map was used to place the circle as one part of something much larger and to hold both the places people have been and the places they would like to go. A World Bank regional map followed, its colour legend offered as a memory aid so an example could be reached for by region rather than by country. The facilitator then walked the sequence the evening would follow: developing the inquiry itself, theories and concepts, how the question is handled around the world rather than only locally, sources and inputs that could build common ground, the opportunities and challenges standing in the way, and a way ahead naming who takes responsibility and reports back. The closing note on the sequence was that the discourse is meant to produce tangible change, which makes accountability and personal responsibility part of the method rather than an afterthought.
beats.pullQuote: But we're moving with collective purpose.
beats.slideHint: Two framing slides - the UN world map, then the colour-coded World Bank regions with the legend called out - followed by the Sequence of Inquiry list (inquiry, theories and concepts, application around the world, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, way ahead) with accountability and personal responsibility along the bottom.

beats.title: Venus as a warning
beats.summary: The floor was opened to whatever anyone wanted to bring, and the first offering was an article comparing Venus with Earth: similar in size, apparently host to life at some point, and, as the article had it, the end state of unchecked global warming - a picture of what Earth could become. It was set against a stated commitment to leaving the earth better for the next generation. The facilitator read it as a warning sign, asked whether humanity only unites with the natural world once the disaster is already inbound and too late to avert, and invited examples of warnings that went unheeded until the consequence arrived. The reply reached for the frog in the boiling water, argued that the water is already boiling and some are being burned, and then refused the despair: media that instils fear paralyses people into fight, flight or freeze, and the warning is more useful taken as an opportunity than as a verdict, because solutions are at hand.
beats.pullQuote: Venus is the result of unchecked global warming.
beats.slideHint: Inquiry-opening slide with Venus and Earth side by side at matching scale, the unchecked global warming line as the caption, and a facing panel showing the frog in boiling water with fight, flight or freeze listed underneath.

beats.title: Having, being, and gratitude for the meal
beats.summary: The article was asked for so it could go in the chat and the context be checked without derailing the discussion. From a podcast conversation with a sustainability practitioner working in nature conservation came a spiritual reading of the problem: economic growth is framed as having and having more, when the emphasis belongs on being, and on a politics of being that helps others flourish. The same account named avoidance as the root - people stay away from uncomfortable truths and deny what is happening in order to feel safe - and treated the discomfort as trauma carried individually, collectively or both, so that feeling it is the precondition for acting on it. The facilitator extended feeling to beings whose language is not understood, arguing that trees, animals and insects are assumed not to feel because they cannot say so, and that humanity as steward should stop treating the world as resources to have and consume. The word resources was proposed for deletion from the vocabulary in favour of taking only what is needed, illustrated by the Japanese phrase said before a meal, itadakimasu, described as gratitude reaching back down the chain from the fish in the river through the fisher, the transporter and the shop to the family table.
beats.pullQuote: people are trying to stay away from uncomfortable truths, from just being uncomfortable.
beats.slideHint: Theories slide with having and being in two columns, the politics of being and the avoidance of uncomfortable truths listed beneath, and an itadakimasu panel drawing the gratitude chain as a single line from river to table.

beats.title: Carbon footprint and the levers of power
beats.summary: A participant picked up how deeply the gratitude practice is embedded in one culture, contrasting societies that describe themselves as melting pots with one where an advanced economy still pauses to thank the chain behind a meal, then widened the frame: climate change read mainly through temperature misses habitats, endangered species and what pollution does to the outcomes of other living things. The facilitator agreed that individual acts matter - cloth bags instead of supermarket plastic, a hybrid instead of a pure gas vehicle - but set them against the people holding the levers over gross tonnage of waste and industrial-scale carbon. The example offered was the first pandemic lockdown, when public infrastructure stopped, the roads emptied, and the haze over Los Angeles lifted; people were amazed to see a blue sky, and the lesson was dropped as soon as ordinary life resumed. The point drawn out was that individual footprints multiplied by population size are the same lever seen from the other end, and that the clear sky was a glimpse of what mindfulness at scale would look like.
beats.pullQuote: Smog City in Los Angeles was gone. You could actually see the sky. It was blue.
beats.slideHint: Theories continued - a two-tier diagram with individual choices (cloth bags, hybrid vehicle) sitting on the industrial and policy tier (gross tonnage of waste, industry-scale carbon), and a lockdown photo pair of a hazy and a clear city skyline.

beats.title: Making the bay matter to the farmer
beats.summary: With a first draft of the question on the screen - cultivating a respect for nature within our communities - the circle turned to a success story. The Chesapeake Bay Foundation, decades in the making, was credited with an effectiveness that comes from making the watershed matter to people at the moment they decide, including people living miles from the water. The worked example was cattle run straight into the creeks, tearing down the banks and fouling the water downstream, against riparian buffer zones sold to farmers on their own terms: less erosion, returning pollinators and wildlife, and either grants for the work or a tax benefit for surrendering a hundred feet on each side of the creek. Nobody was asked to be altruistic; the farmer does what matters most at that moment and the bay wins as a byproduct. A second voice built on that, putting the onus on policy, law and institutions to show that care pays off and to make the benefits of being visible against the habit of taking more, and set beside it a news clip of toxic foam on the Ganges - a river called sacred while waste is allowed into it - weighing profit against what is lost and naming the vote in a democracy as the available lever. A new arrival was welcomed mid-discussion, invited to speak or use the chat, and asked to leave an email address so the written summary of the inquiry could be sent on.
beats.pullQuote: People will do whatever is most important to them at that moment in time
beats.slideHint: Application slide on the watershed: a creek cross-section shown with and without a riparian buffer, an incentive box beside it (grants for the work, tax benefit for a hundred feet each side), and a facing panel on policy levers using the toxic foam on the Ganges as the counter-example.

beats.title: Settling the wording
beats.summary: The facilitator revised the question on the screen and explained the reasoning: policy dictates funding and executive emphasis, sets what an administration deems important, and pushes states and provinces into a fight for federal money; and the framing of the farmer had exposed a reciprocal relationship in which sustaining oneself and improving the watershed benefit the fish, the aquatic life, the grass and the trees together. The revised wording put to the group asked about cultivating a culture of sustainability and reciprocity within our communities, with nature offered as the metaphor for sustainability, and it was repeated once on request. A participant then proposed coexistence in place of reciprocity and read out a version pairing a culture of sustainability with peaceful coexistence with nature; the facilitator answered that peaceful coexistence alone might already contain sustainability, and could be read spiritually or tangibly, which drew agreement that shorter was better. No finished sentence is restated afterwards, so the wording stands as an agreement in the room rather than as anything one person said. Two chat welcomes to the newest arrival landed during this stretch (chat clock 00:57:13 and 00:58:35, recording @36:16 and @37:38), and the river cleaned for the Paris Olympics, named in the room as the Rhine, and the season's tropical storms were raised as live cases.
beats.pullQuote: How do we cultivate a culture of sustainability and reciprocity within our communities?
beats.slideHint: The inquiry slide caught mid-edit: the first draft struck through, the facilitator's sustainability and reciprocity wording in place, the proposed peaceful coexistence with nature variant beside it, and a footnote that the archived question matches neither exactly.

beats.title: Paid time, and the look of good stewardship
beats.summary: Theories and concepts opened with a request for the frames that explain why things are done the way they are, and the watershed came back as the regional driver of environmental behaviour. Clean the bay days were described in detail: agencies and large employers send people out during the workday on excused absence, and the rest of the afternoon is quietly written off. The facilitator turned that into a concept - paid time to volunteer is a commitment an employer makes to employees and to the community at once, it improves wellbeing and engagement, and organisations that do not offer it are hamstringing themselves - and named the two incentives at work, one economic and one cultural. The cultural one was institutional identity: an organisation whose work depends on the water needs to look like a good steward of it, a shift measured against a time when waste went over the side in port and now carries a jail sentence. The same logic ran up to politicians, for whom cleaning the bay is a good bumper sticker because oystermen, fishermen and watermen vote and remember who made harvesting possible again, and back down to the individual who gets a morning on the seawall.
beats.pullQuote: Why would a guy who maybe doesn't have a connection to the bay care about the bay? You got to draw that connection to him.
beats.slideHint: Theories slide with two labelled arrows, economic incentive and cultural identity, running from institution to individual, examples stacked under each (paid volunteer days, excused absence, event sponsorship, political credit, restored oyster harvests), and 'make it important to them' as the header.

beats.title: Incentives, and the record around the world
beats.summary: Incentives and empowerment were named as the mechanism: companies that claim to care should be asked to show it in a form that returns to them, since a stable environment is part of the infrastructure a business runs on and the loop feeds back. Against that, the habit of pushing the onus onto individuals and then onto the young was rejected - people who are overwhelmed and unmotivated cannot be told to work it out alone, and the one useful kind of trickle down is tools, resources, money and incentives reaching the people expected to act. The facilitator added that no individual hero saves humanity; small acts of kindness accumulate into a movement, and once change is tangible people continue for their neighbours and their children. The application recap then gathered the evening's cases: the watershed foundation in the United States, the river cleaned for the Paris Olympics, the Japanese practice of gratitude before a meal, and India's attempt to establish natural rather than human rights for the Ganges, described as stymied by opaque spending, allegations of corruption and bribery, and ineffective governance, while people continue to bathe in the water during yearly purification rituals. A further case came from the Gulf coast of the United States, where chemical plants sited in predominantly African American neighbourhoods drove cancer rates well above neighbouring areas until residents had had enough and pushed back - a David and Goliath fight unlikely to bear fruit for two or three generations, but one where grassroots activism had at least raised the awareness. Asked for successful interventions, the circle answered that the unsuccessful ones are more numerous. The Venus article was located and sent during this stretch, and proved to have come from astronomy.com rather than the news channel first remembered.
beats.pullQuote: Unfortunately, we have more examples of not success.
beats.slideHint: Application world board - a map pinned at the Chesapeake Bay, the Paris Olympic river, Japan, the Ganges and the United States Gulf coast, each pin carrying a one-line outcome, with a tally strip beneath showing more failures than successes.

beats.title: Whose wisdom, and who plants the grass
beats.summary: Treating the world as a resource was named as the thing that turns it into a competition over who owns what. Against that the facilitator set indigenous stewardship - First Nations, Metis and Inuit in Canada, Native Americans in the United States, and equivalents in every region - and argued that the knowledge of how to peacefully coexist with the natural world was lost in the race for industry and the race to progress civilisation, and belongs in policy discussion at every level; the David Suzuki Foundation was named as an organisation working that seam across science, policy, communications and local engagement, with the open difficulty being how to sway large corporations and governments. Canada was offered as a prosperous nation making the attempt and the United States as having some way to go. The sources and inputs section then asked who the circle could learn from, and the answers came from the ground up: a watershed foundation with experts on staff but its real effect at the grassroots, people standing in the water planting oysters and natural grasses, with employers, businesses and youth clubs brought in, and a child wading ankle deep to plant seagrass who will not grasp the impact and does not need to. The facilitator matched it with two lesson-free open school days a year in Canada, when children bring their own things, roam the building and teachers hold classes outdoors in local parks, and asked why that could not become a community garden or a patch of neighbourhood a group takes responsibility for. A local beekeeping club supplied the closest example to the grassroots: volunteers who teach the importance of pollinators to people who will never keep bees, who take calls to collect swarms so the bees are hived rather than killed, and whose work has put beekeeping clubs into nearby schools, with the club trading the space it uses for the upkeep of an observation hive.
beats.pullQuote: not every child is going to be interested in that, but the one or 2 that are they'll they'll change the world for us.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide: a who-can-help column (indigenous knowledge and governance, an environmental foundation, a science and policy nonprofit, local clubs, schools, employers) beside a grassroots photo strip - oyster planting, seagrass, an outdoor school day, an observation hive.

beats.title: Learning sideways
beats.summary: The sources discussion turned to how the work links outward, arguing that this inquiry skips the personal level and plugs straight into community and local government, because bringing in a business, a school or a community group gives an immediate firsthand base of help - as with a school trash pickup that took students around the surrounding neighbourhood. Education was then reframed as a question of framing: teaching that makes people feel bad gets blocked out, while indirect encouragement lands. Two illustrations followed, a bird-song identification app called Merlin, on the argument that recognising which species are around makes a person care whether they survive, and a university alumni day workshop on the microbiome where pond water under a microscope was absorbing enough that an hour was not long enough. Fun and playfulness were named as the vehicle, with policy backing them through schools and through free days to explore nature without much guidance. The facilitator added forest therapy, shinrin-yoku, described as national policy in Japan from the boom years of the 1980s, when a government watching people work themselves to death moved to get them out of offices and back into nature so that they would protect what they had rediscovered enjoying. The practice is aimed at the relationship rather than at the benefits, and it lands differently for people drawn to water and to mountains, but it needs time - which the grind of several jobs and children's activities does not leave, and which an employer can carve out, sowing something people then carry on in their own way.
beats.pullQuote: how much they enjoyed being with nature, and then they'll choose to protect it because they care about it.
beats.slideHint: Sources continued, headed 'indirect beats instruction', with three example cards (bird-song app, pond microbiome under a microscope, unstructured outdoor days) and a shinrin-yoku panel carrying its 1980s policy origin and the note that the practice costs time an employer can supply.

beats.title: What gets in the way
beats.summary: Opportunities and challenges opened on the wisdom of people who have already walked the path: media shows the event and never the years of build-up, whereas a slow grassroots campaign of information sharing and relationship building is what makes an idea ordinary enough for a neighbour to repeat, until keeping bees is a thing people simply talk about. A participant undertook to get that build-up firsthand from the people behind the local beekeeping work, noting that chance conversations there had led to a short interview about not killing pollinators, and that the subject is never left unmentioned. The challenges followed. Competition for resources is ingrained to the point of feeling like common sense, a law of the jungle read into capitalism that has shaped how the Western world approaches the natural world, while countries that took up that fervour less completely write more moderate policy: Singapore was cited for building sustainability into national identity precisely because space is scarce, and Canada for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission that acknowledged at policy level a need for indigenous governance, inviting people in to inform decisions about what gets built and prioritised. Persuading a community already convinced of its own way was named as the uphill climb. The last opportunity was children's activism, opened with the split reaction to Greta Thunberg - dismissed by some as a child or a screamer, treated by others as a model of activism that began with leaving school to sit outside a legislature - and closed on library shelves full of young activists running local environmental projects, with the point that children rightfully have a voice.
beats.pullQuote: if children are able to do this with no resources, what's stopping adults that have plenty of resources to actually make a change for the better
beats.slideHint: Opportunities and Challenges split slide - obstacles on the left (resource competition as common sense, communities already convinced, the invisible build-up behind visible events), openings on the right (learn from practitioners, national models such as Singapore and Canada's commission, youth activism) - with a Greta Thunberg reaction-split panel across the bottom.

beats.title: Way ahead, and a grant in Vancouver
beats.summary: The way ahead asked for someone willing to take the inquiry as a personal responsibility and report back to the forum. One participant took it, undertaking to speak with the local beekeeping volunteers within the week and to bring back the processes rather than the anecdote, along with a report next month on an ongoing volunteering effort. Another suggested inviting one of them into a session, and the offer became a plan to ask about joining for the first half hour of a future gathering. The facilitator volunteered to support the inquiry alongside, then previewed the highlights: a community grant application for a project in Vancouver that would take this online forum into a live monthly event, sited deliberately in a part of the city living with poverty and short of hope, with forest bathing written into the proposal as the healing element. What is learned about process in one country would shape how that project is run in another, starting with neighbours before crossing oceans. The idea of a guest who comes for half an hour was matched to Aristotle's Lyceum, where people walked in, walked alongside and left again rather than being held until the end. Highlights closed with the forum reaching its fifth iteration, storyboards from the previous inquiries available to anyone who asks, and an open invitation for technical suggestions, which drew silence.
beats.pullQuote: You're holding space for healing. And then you're learning together and problem solving.
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead slide naming the carried inquiry, the report-back next month and the possible guest, beside a Highlights panel with the Vancouver grant (monthly in-person Lyceum, forest bathing as the healing element) and the list of previous storyboards available on request.

beats.title: Fellowship circle
beats.summary: The closing round opened with the reminder that silence is itself a form of sharing and nobody is obliged to speak. What came was gratitude: thanks for time and energy given to something wholly voluntary, an acknowledgement of invitees whose schedules had kept them away, and the argument that any project succeeds through the effort of more than one person, with talents counted to include experience, wisdom, education and knowledge. Another voice thanked the group for a discussion that carries on after the call ends, welcomed the two newcomers, hoped the circle would keep widening to people from around the world, and conceded a change of mind about bees. One participant closed with substance rather than pleasantry: sustainability and the environment belong higher on the agenda, the work is largely one of conscience and of educating new generations, and policy should serve the environment and not only business, because people copy what those around them already do - the same cycle visible in the case from India. The facilitator ended on the distinction that makes the forum real: the philosophy is deep, but action is what keeps it from being something mulled over and then slept on, changing those who take part and, through them, the people around them, not by dominating anyone but by embodying something others may choose for themselves. The screen share and the recording were stopped at the end of the round.
beats.pullQuote: I may change my view about bees starting next time.
beats.slideHint: Closing slide with the fellowship circle prompt and the note that silence is also a form of sharing, the round's gratitude lines listed without attribution, and a final panel on choice and freedom with the next gathering and contact details.

inquiries.withheld: Material withheld under the archive's privacy rules: participants' names, relationships between participants, biographical and professional detail from the introductions round, family circumstances, immigration circumstances, health, personal finances, contact details, anything involving a minor, and the names of people who were not present and could not consent.

inquiries.title: A reflection on the past five inquiries, May to November 2024
inquiries.summary: The sixth gathering was a reflection rather than an inquiry. The circle revisited the five inquiries held between May and October 2024, one storyboard at a time, heard from those who had taken each call to action, and then asked one open-ended question each in place of debate. The questions gathered are to be added to the storyboards, so whoever carries an inquiry forward has more to work with.

meeting.landAcknowledgement: No land acknowledgement was given. The opening was a guided series of breaths with gratitude to the earth, to ancestors, to oneself, to family and friends, and to the children who come after. Indigenous knowledge and governance appeared later, inside the recap of the October inquiry on coexistence with nature, not as an acknowledgement of place.
agenda: Welcome, and a reminder of the vision for the endeavor as a philosophy
Collective mindfulness and healing through presence: guided breaths with gratitude prompts
Shared understanding, using the United Nations and World Bank regional maps as a memory prompt for where each person has lived and travelled
The sequence for reflection, with structural and interpersonal norms: respect as the golden rule, about an hour and a half, a raised hand or the chat box to speak
Reflection on the past five inquiries, each one taken as a storyboard overview of about three minutes, then an update from whoever took the call to action, then a questions-only round
Administrative notes on the website, the published storyboards, social media, and a survey tool in development
Fellowship circle for a final moment of sharing
contextNotes: Not an inquiry: a reflection over the five inquiries held between May and October 2024, revisiting each storyboard rather than opening a new question.

The five revisited storyboards covered preparing families for emergencies, a modern work ethic, helping families afford housing, mentoring adolescents into adulthood, and peaceful coexistence with nature.
Announced as special and exploratory; the hosts explained the sequence for reflection as they worked through it, and asked for suggestions on the format.
Two hosts ran the session, scheduled for about an hour and a half; the forum closed at about an hour and twenty minutes.
Each inquiry followed the same pattern: a storyboard overview, an update from whoever had taken the call to action, then questions only.
Questions only means one open-ended question per person, a five Ws or a how question, with no answer expected; the questions are collected to refine and republish the storyboard.
No hands raised was named as a valid choice, and a question could be typed in the chat instead.
Reflective prompts were offered to whoever carries an inquiry: where the volunteering came from, what has shaped the thinking since, and where to go next.
Held on a Sunday, with participants joining at different points of the weekend.
Participants joined from Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia.
Attendance across the earlier gatherings was uneven: one participant had missed all of the prior meetings, and others had attended some and missed others.
One participant joined late after trouble connecting.
Two participants stepped away briefly during the session and returned, each posting a note in the chat.
One participant's microphone carried feedback, and parts of that contribution are unclear in the recording.
The member who had volunteered for two of the calls to action was absent; the hosts undertook to bring the refined storyboards back to that member as encouragement to continue.

Some calls to action had little to report: a planned conversation with a local beekeeper had not happened because of overlapping leave, and accountability to the group was named as the reason for asking anyway.
No survey was run. A survey tool was still in development, with feedback invited through the website or directly to either host.
Administrative notes covered the group's website, theendeavor.net, storyboards published with hyperlinked sources, and social media on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and Quora.

Chat carried material the audio did not: a follow-up placing Virginia's filial responsibility laws in the 1920s, a Los Angeles nonprofit working on housing rights, and reading on AI and the future of work posted near the close and read out by the facilitator.
The meeting was open before recording began, so the recording starts partway in.

The recording continues for about four minutes after the forum closed, with the hosts discussing how to onboard newer members onto the group's collaboration tools; that stretch is administrative and is not part of the record.
No date was announced for the next Lyceum; the hosts stayed on afterwards for follow-up questions.

reviewed.topic: How do we prepare ourselves and our families to handle emergencies? (the 24 May storyboard)
reviewed.discussion: The facilitator walked the storyboard section by section: the Hawaiian concepts of Ohana and Calabash, godparents and a designated support network, extended relatives near and far, the military family care plan and the bug out bag, and differing views in the United States on whether adult children are expected to care for aging parents. Sources and inputs turned on state law differing from federal law, with Virginia and Texas contrasted, and Medicaid raised. Opportunities were the end of life conversations that get put off, on the reasoning that silence transfers stress and financial burden to surviving family. Challenges were the cost of legal advice and the fact that advance care options vary by state or province. The participant who had taken the call to action was absent; a second participant, who had offered to help compile Virginia information, reported back. The circle then moved to questions only. One asked how responsibility is enforced when a death and the next of kin fall in different states, and how that works across an international border. Another agreed that was the same question, saying the within-country rule was easy enough to grasp but cross-border rules were beyond them. A third said something similar exists in China, asked how the Virginia law came about and who started it, and said they disagree with the law and could give philosophical reasons. The facilitator said it is questionable to hold someone legally or financially responsible for what they may not be able to assume, and undertook to carry the refined storyboard back to the absent volunteer so the volunteer knows the group is still working on it.
reviewed.progress: Contact between the two had been brief only. Research had confirmed that Virginia filial responsibility laws are real: an adult child who is able to earn income can be legally obliged to support a parent in need, and failure to support carries a fine of up to 500 dollars and up to 12 months in jail. The participant reporting had been a disbeliever until checking, and said the volunteer who raised it was right. The origin of the law had not been researched - no forensics on how it came to exist - and looking into that was offered as work for the next gathering, jointly with the absent volunteer. Later in the session, roughly 47 minutes into the recording, chat added that Virginia filial responsibility laws date back to the 1920s. Nothing else had been done on this inquiry since May.

reviewed.topic: What should we strive for in a modern work ethic?
reviewed.discussion: The recap set a military and civilian parallel side by side: an anecdote of engineers on a small team being the standouts while the men around them needed more of a guiding hand, contrasted with a medical field where women students were seen as ready and men less so, leading the circle to ask why women are perceived as having to work twice as hard for the same success. Applications were about hiring: whether interview panels and reference checks ask about soft skills, resilience and continuous learning rather than duties performed. Sources and inputs were intercultural skill and the ability to code switch on globalized teams, with a willingness to learn the other person's background treated as a team-building requirement. There was little regulation to draw on, beyond distinguishing the private and public sectors. Opportunities were investment in human capital - paid time off, retirement contributions, and interviewing staff to inform engagement rather than governing by policies written long ago. The challenge recorded was the end of loyalty to a single employer. In questions only, one participant turned the inquiry toward AI: how it will influence a modern work ethic, what the threats are, what it could replace, and whether soft skills keep people ahead. The facilitator asked whether policies written before the rapid increase of technology need overhauling. Another participant answered from government service that the persistent struggle has not been AI but teleworking - the technology exists, the call itself proves it works across the world, smaller organizations have embraced it and found it effective, and larger ones remain slow. Late in the session an essay by the chief executive of Anthropic and a recorded interview with the same author were posted to chat as further reading on AI and work; the facilitator accepted them and said they would be added to this storyboard.
reviewed.progress: The call to action had two strands. The first was a book recommendation, Athena Rising, on how men can act as role models to open opportunity for women; it surfaced again later in the session among mentorship reading. The second strand, conversations with a small team of engineers on a small team about their understanding of continued government service, was reported on at length. The small team the volunteer supervises had met a work environment described as less than supportive rather than toxic: nobody went out of their way to trip them up, and nobody was actively mentoring them, which wrecked havoc on their professional growth. The remedy applied was ordinary mentorship - paying attention, asking questions other than yes or no, taking genuine interest in professional development - and the report was that the team is now thriving and only needs keeping motivated. The origin of that approach was given as an earlier memory: a slight man struggling with a box on the pier would be helped by everyone, and a woman of the same build would be walked past. The specific question the call to action was set up to answer, how the team views continued government service, went unanswered.

reviewed.topic: How can we help families afford housing in our community?
reviewed.discussion: The recap ran through local farmers under-bidding at auction so an evicted family could stay, the scale of the profit incentive in real estate, and tourist destinations where landlords earn more from short term rentals than from permanent residents building wealth through ownership. Applications were Finland's mandates for low rent and rent control, New York City where one generation benefited from affordable housing and the benefit did not pass to the next, and Hampton Roads, where private companies profit from military post housing of questionable quality. Sources and inputs were systemic racism in housing policy by way of The Color of Law, the Fair Housing Act of 1968 and the gap between its passage and its implementation, and homelessness as a multi-spectrum problem - affordable housing, lack of employment, lack of credit converging - so complex that it paralyzes people out of taking part. Policies considered were rent to own, limiting private development in favor of public, and community land trusts letting nonprofits hold land while tenants buy the housing on it. Opportunities were the Broad Creek housing complex in Norfolk, Virginia as a rent to own route, and extending housing benefits to workers in critical fields so they can plant roots rather than commute from a far suburb. The challenge was that housing is an interagency effort mistaken for one agency's sole responsibility. In questions only, one participant asked what incentives Vancouver offers a private owner of a multifamily building to open a percentage of units to people in this situation. The question drew a long silence before any reply. Afterwards the questioner asked whether it had been heard at all, having spoken at length unsure the mute button was off; the facilitator confirmed it had been heard. The reply named no incentive; the facilitator said the storyboard would keep being updated and that this is not Vancouver's problem alone but the future of large population centers unless public and private sectors act together. A Los Angeles nonprofit that works on housing rights was posted to chat and acknowledged in the room about three minutes later.
reviewed.progress: This call to action was carried by one participant, with a view to partnering with organizations addressing poverty in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. Real work had happened. In the first year, the priority had been understanding the environment and who is already there, and using the inputs from the August gathering several nonprofits working with unhoused people had been met, all working together and each approaching it from a different angle. The obstacle brought back was circular: someone recovering from substance use needs employment, employment applications need an address, and an unhoused person has no address. The second finding was that organizations exist to hold nonprofit housing providers and government officials accountable, against the complaint that government money for single room occupancy housing goes to paying employees rather than improving the buildings.

reviewed.topic: How do we mentor adolescents into adulthood? (stated in the room as ages 15 and up)
reviewed.discussion: The recap covered the balance in parenting between freedom and absolute freedom, the theory of constant cultivation that moves children through a checklist of activities, and technology as a surrogate educator whose information is sometimes validated and sometimes not. Applications were responsibility thrust on children early by design or by circumstance, living abroad in Germany increasing autonomy, Japan where young children walking to and from school alone is a cultural norm, and a caregiver gap in the United States created by military training and deployment, which creates a condition for poverty. Sources and inputs were negotiation as a life skill and the question of when children get to negotiate for autonomy, and whether surrogate mentors arrive when a caregiver is absent - and whether their absence creates harmful coping mechanisms carried into adulthood. Policies were flexible work and paid time off as a route to parental involvement beyond weekends and holidays. Opportunities and challenges were volunteer mentorship near schools, the varying quality of social media platforms and when to teach a safe presence online, learning what today's youth actually like rather than demanding they learn what an earlier generation learned, and a shortage of mentors in all communities. In questions only the facilitator asked whether any organization carries mentorship across the line into legal adulthood, calling 18 to 28 a vulnerable stretch because decisions now carry legal consequences, and whether organizations pass the torch from 17 into 18 and beyond. One participant said programs for that band would have to be researched. Another made a plug for earlier interdiction: a terrible decision at 16 is permanent in certain jurisdictions, and mentoring a child after a life altering decision, or from behind bars, is a poor substitute for mentoring before it. A third accepted the point as proactive rather than reactive and asked what criteria organizations actually use to designate at-risk youth - whether a young person must already have deviated or been caught, or whether some other factor identifies risk before anything has gone wrong. A fourth proposed that mentoring start before students leave high school, with a professional inside the school to talk to and to encourage a young person to find what interests them, noting that in some communities a counselor is hard to come by. The facilitator cited student support services in Canada as an example, asked what happens when a school has no such staff or one guidance counselor for an entire student body, and recalled military recruiters coming into a high school in a military town, asking what the comparable outside visitors are in towns that get none.
reviewed.progress: Two participants had taken this call to action and one was absent, so the plan to research how communities from local to international scale address mentoring, using social media, went unreported. The other reported a real survey of what already exists, done by reading, general internet search and ordinary community involvement. Mentoring organizations turned out to be plentiful and mostly aimed at at-risk youth and high school ages: the YMCA, state behavioral health services, the Up Center, the Boys and Girls Club of America, and Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts. The Up Center's Team UP was singled out as dating only from 2008 and covering ages 6 to 17. The shape of the commitment was described as a mentor signing up, being matched with a mentee, and giving a couple of hours a week, through government at state, federal or city level, through school systems, or through nonprofits. The route in most often runs through activities already close at hand; this participant had become a volunteer official with USA Swimming and now gives several hours a month to officiating meets. Alongside the organizational route, the report described direct conversation with young people about their use of social media, what they study, what they want after high school - college, a vocational program - and money, noting that a first car is the immediate goal and saving toward a house or any longer-term aim had not occurred to them. Reading on mentorship was offered to the group, and the participant undertook to take the evening's questions back into further research. One planned strand, looking into a school unit, had not been done.

reviewed.topic: How do we cultivate peaceful coexistence with nature in our communities?
reviewed.discussion: The recap was drawn from international examples: the Ganges in India as a holy site flooded with toxic waste from industry and from religious ceremony, and Venus as a planet once like Earth whose atmosphere changed until it was uninhabitable, offered as a possible warning. Applications were India using the court system to extend rights to land, water and air as human rights are understood, and the Chesapeake Bay Foundation in Virginia building a grassroots culture of care for a watershed regardless of a person's industry or private life. Sources and inputs were an uncomfortable truth - a psychological barrier against discomfort leads people to disengage from a complex problem that is happening to them, which limits their citizenship - and the need for those holding the levers of power, corporations and governments, to lead by example. Policies included the contrast between Los Angeles before Covid and during it, when the sky was visible and there was less smog, and environmental racism, where marginalized populations carry greater health hazards through unclean drinking water or land too contaminated to farm. Opportunities were increasing indigenous governance so indigenous knowledge shapes policy, with the David Suzuki Foundation in Canada named as a champion of that, and conservation taught through routine play and exploration inside the school curriculum. Challenges were engaging the older population for cultural wisdom to pass on, and the poor fit between collectivist ideas and communities leaning into purely capitalist thought. An administrative change was reviewed alongside this storyboard: it was the first to carry hyperlinks to the underlying material, the summaries are being hung on the group's website, and the circle was asked for suggestions on the format and for anything that would improve it. The facilitator closed the section by asking whether organizations in government and people in the private sector using their wealth for sustainability are being highlighted in the media in a way that draws others in, or whether those examples are lost to a current atmosphere of fear that prevents shared understanding on climate change. No further questions came.
reviewed.progress: Nothing had happened. The call to action was to speak with a local beekeeper, a work associate of one participant, about how the protection of pollinators is organized and encouraged, and to ask whether the beekeeper would come to a future gathering to speak. The two had not connected: one had been on leave, then the other, and follow-up was deferred until a return to work. The facilitator accepted this and restated the purpose - that the group helps hold each other accountable to what its members say they will do - and repeated the invitation for the beekeeper to join for a short stint.

learned.text: The reflection ran as an untested format. A sequence for reflection stood in place of the Sequence of Inquiry, and the facilitator said so openly rather than presenting it as settled practice.
Reflection exists to hold the circle accountable. Revisiting an inquiry is how a volunteer is reminded of what was undertaken.
Questions only produces refinement rather than answers. Questions harvested from the circle are folded back into the storyboard, which is then republished for whoever carries the call to action.
Silence is a sanctioned response. Raising no hand counts as participation, and the chat box is an equal route into the record.
Volunteers arrive with little or nothing to report, and the format absorbs that rather than penalising it. Of five calls to action revisited, one had barely started and one had stalled entirely.
Life outside the circle is treated as an expected cause of stalled work, not a failure of the volunteer.
Attendance is intermittent, and the reflection serves the people who missed gatherings. Participants who had been absent said the retrospective let them reach inquiries they had not been present for.

carried.text: The facilitators undertook to carry the refined storyboard and the circle's new questions back to the absent volunteer holding the family emergencies inquiry.
One participant undertook to research the origins of the filial responsibility laws, with the volunteer holding that inquiry, in time for the next gathering.
The participant carrying the housing inquiry undertook to keep updating its storyboard as the work in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside continues.
One participant undertook to fold the circle's new questions on at-risk criteria and early intervention into further research, and to report back on the mentorship inquiry.
One participant observed that provision for the band above seventeen would have to be researched; nobody undertook it in the room.
One participant renewed an undertaking to approach a local beekeeper about speaking at a future Lyceum on protecting pollinators, after leave on both sides prevented contact.
The facilitators undertook to add reading contributed through the chat on AI and the future of work to the work ethic storyboard.

changed.text: Reflection becomes an ongoing part of the cycle. Volunteers carrying a call to action are expected to give a short update against set reflective prompts on where they started, what has shifted their thinking, and where to go next.
Storyboards now carry hyperlinks to their sources, and the session summaries are published on the endeavor's website.
Storyboards will also be sent to participants by email on request.
A survey tool is under development to gather structured feedback through subsequent gatherings, alongside the message form already on the website.
The circle was asked directly to propose changes to the reflection format itself, not only to the inquiries.
An onboarding team and a written checklist are to be created for bringing new members onto the group's collaboration platform.

openQuestions.text: Whether filial responsibility obligations follow a person across state lines, and what applies at all when family members are in different countries.
How the filial responsibility laws came about, who pushed for them, and what the argument was at the time.
What AI does to a modern work ethic, which skills it displaces and which it cannot reach. The question was put and not answered; the one response spoke to teleworking instead.
Whether Vancouver offers private multifamily owners any incentive to open a share of units to people who are unhoused. Asked, and left unanswered.
Whether any mentorship carries past seventeen, or whether organisations hand the relationship off into legal adulthood, when decisions first carry legal consequence.
What criteria mark a young person as at risk, and whether the designation follows harm already done or can precede it.
Whether government and private sector sustainability examples reach the public at all, or are lost to the present atmosphere of fear.
How to bring in members who do not use the collaboration platform the core group runs on. Named as the group's largest present obstacle.
Whether a modern work ethic requires overhauling company and organizational policies written before the rapid increase of technology.
