beats.title: Presence circle, and the reflection cadence
beats.summary: Presence opens the circle with breathing borrowed from an indigenous Hawaiian group, awakened Aloha. Breath is offered as a way to express spirituality and shared connection. Five breaths of gratitude: the earth, ancestors, kindness to oneself, families and friends, children. Stress and baggage are exhaled before the discourse begins. Recap of the November 17 gathering, a six-month reflection across five previous inquiries. That gathering questioned each steward rather than answering anything new. Reflection continues at six-month intervals; 2025 restarts the sequence from the top. Inquiries are described as individual journeys held up by a collective that may live elsewhere.
beats.slideHint: Presence slide with the five gratitude breaths, then a look back at the six-month reflection.
beats.pullQuote: It is to give them a chance to have a better future, and it is through our example that we set, that we can give them that chance to pursue their life of meaning and collective purpose.

beats.title: Shared understanding round
beats.summary: The floor opens for introductions on four prompts: name, cultural identity, home, and connection to the Lyceum. What the round establishes: a circle spanning Los Angeles, Belize and Central America, Hawaii, and Northern Virginia, which mostly describes itself as multicultural rather than as one nationality. Routes in vary, among them an online course, networking, and existing personal connection. Growth noted: further participants meant to attend and are expected next time, from more backgrounds. The Lyceum is placed in the 18 hundreds as an American form of adult education. Its subject then was active citizenship and what it means to be human; the aim now is to make that relevant again.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding prompts: name, cultural identity, where you live, connection to the Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: it's something that had existed in the United States in the 18 hundreds.

beats.title: World framing, then a topic arrives
beats.summary: United Nations map shown as the highest level of human organization. Its borders are political lines that politics can smudge or erase quickly. People on the ground may perceive their world differently from the paper. World Bank region colors give the circle a way to place a story when the country is not named. Sequence of Inquiry recapped, with lived experience held to be more than theory. The slide then becomes editable, inviting a topic rather than a finished question. A former president's post-presidency is offered, days after his death at a hundred. Habitat for Humanity is already familiar in the room, from volunteering with it once. A line attributed to Maya Angelou anchors why the example still carries feeling.
beats.slideHint: UN world map and the World Bank region map, then Sequence of Inquiry and an empty inquiry box.
beats.pullQuote: probably better known as what he did after his presidency than what he did during his presidency.

beats.title: What the eulogies revealed
beats.summary: Habitat for Humanity was the surface knowledge; the eulogies filled in the rest. Guinea worm eradication surprises the circle, and one voice had seen the parasite's effects firsthand. No pharmaceutical heroics were needed - clean up the water, and everyone bought in. Minority status in his own Georgia hometown is raised as formative. He volunteered to room with the first African American student to enter the Academy. Election monitoring in impoverished areas is added, done as a couple rather than alone. Public image described as an instrument used for humanity's sake. A claim that no missile was dropped during his tenure is offered and flagged as unverified.
beats.slideHint: Inquiry slide filling with story fragments; the humanitarian work under discussion.
beats.pullQuote: It really just took, you know. Let's say, let's clean up the water folks, and everyone bought into it.

beats.title: Earlier evidence of the same character
beats.summary: The circle looks earlier than the presidency for the same disposition. Navy in World War Two, the Naval Academy, submarines, then the early nuclear program. Volunteered to be lowered into a melted-down reactor in Canada so it could be shut down. One voice doubts being willing to do the same, and calls the act crazy. He required the service academies to integrate women, the year before one class entered. Integration on gender followed integration on race, imperfectly but committed to. Genuineness and spiritual faith named as the constant under all of it. A racist father is countered by following a mother's example instead. Scientist and peanut farmer at once, with no separation between the two roles.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts opening, tracing one life backward for its formative acts.
beats.pullQuote: You're a scientist as well as a farmer, so there is. There was no difference for him in those things, because he was doing something important.

beats.title: The question takes shape
beats.summary: Values are pulled out of the stories: doing what is right, being genuine, looking out for others' welfare. Cultural awareness noted - dialogue rather than dominating with one way of thinking. A question is typed into the box, explicitly not set in stone. One reading answers it with volunteering to give back. Impact is described as permeating outward from the individual to city, state, and federal levels. Sphere of influence should extend past the house into the local community. The facilitator offers a counterpoint: the same values can be carried inside an official capacity. Recognition without announcement - the title was never the credential. Consensus reached to proceed, with tweaks allowed as the sequence runs.
beats.slideHint: The inquiry box now filled in: how can we embody the values of a humanitarian in our communities?
beats.pullQuote: he didn't walk around saying, I am former president, Jimmy Carter. This is why I'm doing what I do.

beats.title: Theories: innate, learned, or mixed
beats.summary: One theory holds the disposition innate - simply who the person already was. Another asks what life experiences and what teaching produced it. The example's own father is raised as a spur toward becoming something different. The example's mother, active in the community, was noticed and became an influence. A prison card ratio is offered: mothers' day cards far outnumbered fathers' day cards. The facilitator declines to settle it on genetics alone. Personality, family example, community, and formative experience are folded together instead. Adolescence and the years after high school are named as the shaping window.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts, listing innate nature, learned behavior, and formative experience.
beats.pullQuote: Mothers have a huge impact on, on, on men.

beats.title: Examples from other countries
beats.summary: The circle is asked for parallels from outside the United States. Terry Fox named for Canada: cancer, a lost leg, and a run coast to coast. The goal was one dollar from every Canadian, about twenty million at the time. Angry drivers who did not know what he was doing exposed a language barrier. He could not finish, and died without the cancer resources available today. Bob Marley named as a worldwide humanitarian, remembered through stories that circulated. Returning wealthy to the poor part of Jamaica, doors left open for anyone to come in. Never the type to say this is mine; a partner is credited with the legacy too. Approachability is contrasted with hero worship that lifts a person out of community.
beats.slideHint: Application slide gathering examples by country: Canada, Jamaica, the United States.
beats.pullQuote: The goal itself wasn't the important thing, because, like, unfortunately, Terry Fox didn't complete it. But that example inspired the nation, and it continues to inspire it today.

beats.title: From heroic stature to pillar of community
beats.summary: A recently deceased local figure is offered as the same pattern at neighborhood scale, no longer at heroic stature. The reach crossed religious, cultural, and economic lines wherever help was needed. Problems were brought to this person, who convened others and, when that failed, did the work directly. Local and colloquial rather than headline-grabbing, and with no interest in headlines. The circle stops wishing for such a person and finds one already named. The facilitator renames pillar of society as pillar of community. What to study is specified: what they do, how they speak, how they treat people. Pairs recur across the examples, and a pair aligned on one shared passion is described as multiplying what either could do alone.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs, with local pillars of community listed beside the national figures.
beats.pullQuote: we've taken somebody that's almost, you know, a heroic stature like Jimmy Carter, and we've narrowed it. We've brought it down to our community

beats.title: Nature and nurture, and institutions as bridges
beats.summary: Nature versus nurture is rejected as a false choice; both mold who a person becomes. Another pairing is added, crediting a musician's wife with carrying the legacy outward. Father Boyle named as a local humanitarian influencer in Los Angeles. The meeting came about through a class that its instructor took out into community events. Academic institutions are credited with connecting people to living examples, not only to papers. That encounter stayed with one participant and reached this circle years later. The facilitator proposes assembling a straw man of the humanitarian from across regions. Attention shifts from the finished person to the building blocks that made them.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs, adding institutions and mentors, with nature and nurture paired not opposed.
beats.pullQuote: an academic institution is studying a particular subject, and they're connecting people from that institution with community.

beats.title: Suffering as the trigger
beats.summary: Seeing others suffer draws out the wish to help; not seeing it leaves the comfort zone intact. Discrimination by race and gender is recalled as moving the example under discussion even though it never touched him directly. The Los Angeles fires are named as a live wake-up call rather than an abstraction. Struggle is described as honing resilience that can then be lent to others. Failure is offered as the best teacher, and lived experience alongside it. An African proverb is cited - experience teaches once a thing has been felt. Own struggle and witnessed suffering are joined: empathy comes from both. Chat carries a reminder to mute microphones, as feedback is reaching the audio.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts revisited, adding suffering, struggle, and failure as inputs.
beats.pullQuote: when we don't see it, then we just live in our comfort zone. But then we want to step out and help others.

beats.title: When suffering hardens instead
beats.summary: A harder question is put to the group: suffering can harden a person, not soften them. Some who came through it tell the next person to get through it too. Another layer must explain who steps in and helps rather than moving on. The fires answer part of it - loss reaches celebrities and apartment dwellers alike. Losing possessions also means losing the memories built into a home. Loss is named as universal among humans, independent of wealth. Equality is reframed from access to opportunity into shared vulnerability. Empathy is proposed as the favorable quality that makes the difference. Empathy has been seen developing later in life, so it may be changeable by decision.
beats.slideHint: Favorable and Unfavorable columns, with empathy entered on the favorable side.
beats.pullQuote: I think the difference is, the favorable quality is empathy.

beats.title: Modelling empathy, and the economics of time
beats.summary: The question turns to how parents and caregivers demonstrate empathy to the young. Children who watch adults tear at each other learn that dialogue is impossible. Pillars of community make themselves known, and are recognized regardless of age. Nobody can be forced into empathy, but conditions for choosing it can be created. Economic framing is named as itself divisive, arguing systems instead of connection. Survival paycheck to paycheck leaves no energy left over for community. The facilitator asks whether every example so far comes from the upper strata. One participant holds firmly that economic status does not matter at all. Another argues achieved status bought flexibility and freedom from worry. The two are reconciled: means widen the reach, but the disposition came first.
beats.slideHint: Favorable and Unfavorable, with economic circumstance and available time entered as challenges.
beats.pullQuote: people who want to help are going to help, because there's always somebody that is, who's down on their luck that can use some help.

beats.title: A counterexample, then the call to action
beats.summary: Cesar Chavez is offered as a humanitarian who was poor for most of his life. A farm worker who organized for workers' rights and union representation in California. His rallying cry is traced forward into a later presidential campaign. Dolores Huerta is added as the organizing partner, another pairing. Affluence makes the work easier but is judged not to be required. One participant volunteers to research what volunteering looks like in the Hampton Roads area. Another volunteers to support, sending parallel examples from California. A shared document is agreed for comparing pillars of community east and west. The facilitator frames it as an individual journey held up by the group.
beats.slideHint: Call to Action, recording a steward, a supporting member, and a shared east-west document.
beats.pullQuote: It could be a very nice experiment of East, East and West, right to see what's happening on the East coast versus what's happening on the west coast

beats.title: Learning reflection and fellowship circle
beats.summary: The learning reflection opens with a three-question QR code on screen. Survey links are posted in the chat for the participant who cannot scan from a phone. The forms stay open, so nobody needs to finish before the closing. The fellowship circle opens for one final round, with silence counted as a contribution. Thanks offered for being allowed to bring a local example to the group. One post-survey answer is read out into the circle: humbled. Humbled by the humanitarians discussed, and by the wisdom of this group. The facilitator notes the examples span government, entertainment, and the local level. It has been done, so it can be done, and others can be inspired to it. The closing thought sets fear of overstepping against the courage to reach a hand out.
beats.slideHint: Learning Reflection QR code with three questions, then the Fellowship Circle closing slide.
beats.pullQuote: it could be nothing, you know silence is also a contribution

inquiries.withheld: Material withheld under the archive's privacy rules: participants' names, relationships between participants, biographical and professional detail from the introductions round, family circumstances, immigration circumstances, health, personal finances, contact details, anything involving a minor, and the names of people who were not present and could not consent.

provenance.source: the meeting recording transcript and the chat log

inquiries.inquiry: How do we advocate for healthcare equity in our communities?

meeting.landAcknowledgement: None on the record. The recording begins after the opening the facilitator refers back to, and no land gratitude is spoken during the session.
agenda: Open floor to surface topics and narrow the inquiry question for the day
Group confirmation of the agreed question by thumbs up before proceeding
Theories and concepts, drawing on lived experience rather than expert testimony
Applications, then sources and inputs: who to consult about the causes
Opportunities and challenges arising from the discussion
Call to action, with a volunteer and a second to carry the inquiry forward
Learning reflection questions on screen, answered by phone, with no deadline
Closing fellowship circle, where silence itself counts as a contribution
contextNotes: Held online over Zoom; the recording runs from the start of the inquiry to @1:09:22.
Recording begins after the opening; the norms round and any pre-survey are not on it.
Topic was not pre-determined; the circle surfaced and agreed the question in the first eight minutes.
Circle spanned two countries: three joined from Canada and two from the United States at the outset.
A sixth participant joined a few minutes in and was brought up to speed on the question.
One further person joined in the final minute, after the closing had begun, and is not counted.
The facilitator called the technical trouble a first and asked the circle's patience.
Sequence of Inquiry ran theories, lived experience, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, and call to action.
A storyboard of the inquiry was promised to the circle for use in later Lyceums.
Comparison across the United States, Canada, Japan, and England ran through the whole session.
Learning reflection questions were displayed on screen rather than read aloud, so their wording is not recoverable.

theories.text: Healthcare framed as a right rather than a privilege or a tiered social system.
One insurance plan, unequal tiers: an extended dependent covered worse than the immediate family.
Care regardless of finances is a World Health Organization and UN aim, not an enshrined right.
In the United States, health insurance commercializes the provision of care.
Many in the United States want the universal care Canada promises, staffing limits included.
No standardization of medicine prices: hospitals set their own price points.
Under full coverage, patients have no sense of what their own care costs.
Enrollment is not access: both systems grant coverage they cannot always deliver.
Both systems handle emergencies; failure concentrates in routine and non-emergent care.
Information, not money alone, makes choice possible; without it patients accept what is offered.
Upfront payment, more than the later bill, is what turns people away from care.
Geography and plan tier decide access; a move can change the care available.
Unresolved: whether commercial incentive raises standards or is itself the defect.
Uncovered cost does not vanish; it shifts to public institutions or to forgone care.

applications.text: European systems: care broadly free at the point of use, funded by government.
Japan ranked third in the world for healthcare quality against cost.
Japan: a Blue Cross Blue Shield letter of guarantee was not honored by the hospital.
Japan: non-citizens outside the national insurance system faced narrower prescribing options.
Japan: patients were seen quickly, without the long waits reported in Canada.
Canada: universal coverage meant urgent, serious treatment carried no cost to the patient.
England's National Health Service, relayed secondhand: about $50,000 a year for each person.
Each visit draws that pot down, roughly $275 for a doctor, making costs visible.
The pot is topped up when it empties, so nobody is turned away.

sources.text: An economist or healthcare administrators could be brought in for expert perspective.
A contact who can explain coverage for extended family members beyond the household.
Personnel data: accreditation numbers, and whether nurses are leaving the medical field.
A subject-matter expert from an insurance provider, or a practicing medical professional.
A provincial data repository and the local health authority, instead of random clinic calls.
Care navigation starts with a general practitioner who has connections and refers onward.
Plain summaries of what coverage to expect later, instead of hours of research.
Public education on universal healthcare, so a wider audience can weigh it.
Hospitals and providers disclosing standard prices for procedures and medicines.
Canadian versus American hospital billing overhead, a secondhand comparison needing verification.
Anonymized cost data by age group, showing which interventions people typically need.
Session notes shared with the volunteers as the starting point for research.
Doctors Without Borders: how care is administered, and who pays for it.
Contacts in other countries, including African countries, to be asked directly.
Post-survey responses requested from participants by a link in the chat.
A need for prices published before care, not an explanation of benefits weeks later.
A need for plain-language coverage guidance, sparing families hours of unpaid research.
A need for workforce evidence: why practitioners leave, and why general practice attracts few.
Scope-of-practice rules by jurisdiction: who may serve as primary provider decides supply.
Several of the comparisons rest on half-remembered figures and need verifying before use.
A like-for-like comparison of how peer nations fund, price and deliver care.
What coverage applies across a border, for travelers and for new residents alike.
A standing shared document, so a later inquirer starts from collected knowledge.

policies.text: Hippocratic oath - taught as a duty to treat regardless of socioeconomic status.
TRICARE Plus - a dependent tier seen only at military facilities, not other hospitals or urgent care.
TRICARE Select - permits care from providers outside the military system.
Medicare becomes the primary provider in a retiree's sixties, with TRICARE reduced to a supplement.
Medicare parts A, B, C and D - a split routinely confused with Medicaid.
BC nurse line, 8-1-1 - a provincial program giving nurse guidance by phone.
Health authorities - British Columbia divided into regions that set where care is sought.
Provinces and states set their own health regulations; federal matters stay uniform.
Scope of practice - some states will not accept a nurse practitioner as a general practitioner.
Jails are required to provide and pay for the medical care of people in custody.
Universal health care - Canada's promise, named as an aspiration for the United States.
Stated doctrine: health care should carry no insurance and should not be commercialized.

opportunities.text: Circle spanning two countries supplies an immediate comparison of two healthcare systems.
Care navigation starts with a general practitioner who knows where and when to refer.
Arriving with a written list of questions makes the appointment work.
Nurse practitioners can hold the primary-care role where physicians are unavailable.
Military coverage, examined openly, could show civilians a model that already works.
Mixed ages in the circle surface later-life coverage questions before they arrive.
Offered the choice, patients could weigh a shorter wait against surgical experience.
Disclosed standard prices for procedures and medicines would end blind shopping for care.
Other prosperous nations already standardize coverage, offering the United States a working model.
A yearly notional care allowance would show costs while nobody gets turned away.
Anonymized patterns of care by age group would let common needs be anticipated.
The military health system runs a comparable nurse hotline, so the model exists twice.
Video assessment by phone could route people to the right care, saving money.
Public terminals, a library for instance, extend remote care to those without devices.
Commercial incentive phases out weak doctors and keeps competent ones in the system.
In-person Lyceums in local communities would sidestep the online platform barriers.
Nurse-led phone triage, proven in two systems, is the cheapest relief for crowded emergency rooms.

challenges.text: Health insurance held in one country may not cover care received in another.
An unexpected medical expense can financially ruin a family's retirement and savings.
Under one tier of Tricare, a dependent can be seen only for emergencies at military facilities.
A non-emergency operation took six months to reach a surgeon and eight months to complete.
Support may be lacking for treating access to medical care as a fundamental human right.
A nationwide shortage of doctors leaves long emergency waiting lines across Canada.
Commercial standards in health care fail to meet the actual ethical intent.
Scarce doctors push routine cases into emergency rooms meant for life, limb and eyesight.
End-of-life and long-term care costs more, and coverage must be taken in the right window.
Upfront payments and copays keep better programs out of reach on lower incomes.
Hospitals set their own prices: two across the street charged differently for the same medication.
The shortest waiting time can mean the least experienced surgeon.
Some are willing to commit a crime to get access to medical services.
The bill arrives a week to a month after care, too late to weigh cost.
Remote triage assumes cameras and connectivity that not everyone has.
People do not go to the hospital simply because they have no money for it.
Waiting is itself a health cost: pain, lost activity, lifetime impact.
Two publicly funded programs, separately administered, must be reconciled by the patient.
Named barriers: legal red tape, commercialization, personnel shortage, insurance friction deterring practitioners.

inquiries.quote: There's people that don't go to the hospital just because they don't have money for it.
inquiries.callToAction: Two participants took the inquiry forward, both volunteering on the night. The participant who raised the question undertook to research it and start a document, with no fixed starting point: how healthcare is administered in other countries, including several in Africa, and how Doctors Without Borders delivers care and who funds it. That work is to stay general rather than follow every rabbit hole. The same participant asked that the facilitator's notes from the session be shared with the group on Teams. A second participant volunteered to partner on it and to act as a sounding board for questions between this Lyceum and the next. A shared collaborative document is to be created and the two volunteers connected to it, so that anyone arriving later with the same question starts from the circle's collected wisdom rather than a blank slate, and a storyboard of the session is to be produced for subsequent Lyceums. Survey links are to be emailed to anyone who could not reach the on-screen QR code or the chat. Three of those present undertook to note the evening's technical difficulties and refine how the online Lyceum is delivered.

storyboard.logline: Six voices in the United States and Canada spent an hour comparing two healthcare systems and asking whether care is a right, a privilege, or a commercial product.
storyboard.arcNotes: The recording starts after the meeting opened, so the introduction, the norms and the pre-survey are not on it, and neither is the first stretch of troubleshooting for a participant dialling in by phone, which is referred to later from memory. The question was not pre-determined: the first six minutes are the circle building one out of an opening story, a keywords round, and a right-versus-privilege framing, with agreement taken by thumbs up before the inquiry proper. The two-word phrase that names the whole session lands at a cue boundary the transcript attributes unreliably, so the record does not credit 'healthcare equity' to any voice. From there the evening ran the standard sequence: theories and concepts on lived experience, application across the United States, Canada, Japan and England, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, a call to action with two volunteers, then the learning reflection and the fellowship circle. Convergence came late and on process rather than ideology: disclose standard prices, give people the information to choose, and let a person see what their own care costs. The strongest disagreement in the room, and the most useful, was over commercialisation - one position wanted insurance abolished, another credited commercial incentive with the standards that draw medical students from other countries.

beats.title: Opening the floor
beats.summary: The facilitator framed the forum as the place to raise a question that has been mulling, and to problem solve it as collective wisdom rather than alone, then opened the floor with no topic set. The first proposal was a comparison of medical insurance and medical systems between countries, contrasting European systems where care is broadly free and subsidised by government with the American arrangement. Alongside it came a second-hand account of a visitor whose emergency treatment abroad was not covered by home-country insurance, offered as evidence that not knowing the financial system you are entering carries a real cost, on vacation or in residence. The facilitator accepted the story and asked for it to be narrowed to the level of families in a community.
beats.pullQuote: This is the Forum that we can raise a question, something that we've been mulling over.
beats.slideHint: Title slide for the February Lyceum, then the empty inquiry slide with the sequence of inquiry listed down the side and the question line left blank, showing that the topic was still being built.

beats.title: Building the question
beats.summary: Asked for keywords, the circle moved from insurance to entitlement: healthcare as a human right, the right to survive, basic emergency coverage, and whether care is a right, a privilege, or a tiered system, at local level or worldwide. The phrase healthcare equity was landed on here. The facilitator noted the circle already spanned two countries, two participants in the United States and three in Canada, so a comparison of two national approaches was unavoidable, and framed the stakes in household terms, an unexpected medical expense being able to end a family's retirement and savings. A distinction between emergent and non-emergent care was flagged for later. A late arrival was brought up to speed, the question was stated back to the circle, and agreement was taken by thumbs up before the inquiry began. One participant made the stakes concrete with a surgery bill in five figures that insurance absorbed.
beats.pullQuote: How do we advocate for healthcare equity in our communities?
beats.slideHint: Inquiry slide with the question filled in, a keywords cloud from the deliberation (right, privilege, tiered system, emergency coverage, human right), and a two-country marker for the United States and Canada.

beats.title: Lived experience over theory
beats.summary: The facilitator opened theories and concepts by setting lived experience above theory: an economist or a healthcare administrator could be brought in, but what the circle and the people around it have actually been through gives a truer sense of how these systems land. Experience of three national systems was put into the room, with perceived quality rising with each move, alongside a ranking placing Japan third in the world for healthcare quality at cost. That comparison produced the section's sharpest structural point: an American insurer's letter of guarantee was acknowledged but not honoured by a hospital abroad, which demanded cash up front and left reimbursement to be recovered afterwards through paperwork. The concern drawn from it was for any family told to pay a large sum before treatment, forced to weigh a payment against protecting a life.
beats.pullQuote: I wouldn't want that to be the norm for any family that had to decide between how you're going to make a payment.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: lived experience above theory, with a three-country strip for the United States, Japan and Canada, and a callout that a letter of guarantee is not the same thing as coverage.

beats.title: Coverage that changes with the address
beats.summary: The Hippocratic oath, recalled as a duty to treat without regard to socioeconomic status, was offered as the reason care sits closer to a right than a privilege. Against that, the round set out how coverage changes inside one country: under the United States military health plan the tier a dependent is enrolled at decides what care is reachable, and a secondary dependent moved to a different region of the plan could not be registered with a primary care physician, could not get a hospital or service enrolment, and could be seen only at a military facility and only for emergencies, with a queue everywhere else. Conversations and phone calls did not shift it. The conclusion offered was that the system is overburdened rather than malicious, that where a person lives decides what care they can reach, and that the Canadian counterpart is a months-long wait for elective surgery.
beats.pullQuote: the system is, you know, seemingly overburdened.
beats.slideHint: Application slide comparing plan tiers within one country: what a primary enrollee gets against what a secondary dependent gets, with 'emergency only, at one facility' called out and a wait-time comparison against Canada.

beats.title: What waiting costs
beats.summary: Asked directly whether long waits are real, the Canadian side of the circle confirmed them from experience: roughly six months to see a surgeon and around eight to reach a non-emergency operation, with pain limiting ordinary activity throughout the interval, so the wait is itself a health cost rather than a delay. The circle also noted that the same system produces wildly different waits, apparently tracking which provider and which surgeon is available rather than need alone. Two persistent problems were named as the substance of the Canadian experience: finding a primary care physician and then holding on to one before that physician retires, and getting non-emergency surgery done in a reasonable time, with the least waiting and the least lifetime impact.
beats.pullQuote: finding your your doctor, your your primary care physician, and then holding on to them.
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide on access: a timeline bar showing six months to consultation and eight to operation, beside the two named problems - find and keep a primary physician, and get non-urgent surgery in reasonable time.

beats.title: A right, or a commercial product
beats.summary: The provision of care regardless of financial circumstance was put forward as a good norm and as what the World Health Organization and the United Nations strive for, with the honest caveat that it may not be enshrined as a human right and that many countries do not provide it as a matter of course. In the United States, the argument ran, the health insurance system commercialises the provision of care, and whatever ethical goal medical providers subscribe to through the Hippocratic oath does not trump how the profession operates commercially. The problem was placed alongside the lack of housing for the unhoused as a challenge of the same order. Doubt was expressed that enough support exists for access to care without either a third-party insurer or out-of-pocket payment, and broadening coverage for those most in need was offered as the realistic target.
beats.pullQuote: our health insurance system is commercializing the provision of care.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide two: is care a right - World Health Organization and United Nations aspiration on one side, commercialised provision on the other, with the unhoused comparison as a footnote and 'broaden coverage for those most in need' as the landing line.

beats.title: Shortage across a whole country
beats.summary: The facilitator asked whether care differs by region, coast to coast in the United States and province to province in Canada. The answer distinguished the two layers: provinces and states regulate, mandate and organise differently, while federal matters should be uniform, but a shortage of physicians and long emergency waiting lines are common right across the country rather than local. That shortage was traced through to its consequences inside clinics and community health centres, which reorganise and reshuffle roles to keep providing service, with burnout, missed detail and incidents of accident as the foreseeable result if the burden is not relieved. A line posted in the chat added that the commercial reality of healthcare standards fails to meet the actual ethical intent, logged at chat clock 00:28:07, which is @23:22 on the recording.
beats.pullQuote: one thing across Canada is that there is a shortage of of doctors that we have
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide on structure: federal against provincial and state regulation, with a national shortage banner across both and a consequence chain from shortage to reshuffled roles to burnout and error.

beats.title: Five candidate causes
beats.summary: A cross-country comparison of prescribing opened the stretch: not paying into a national insurance system limited which medications could be prescribed, a later move allowed a better fit, and the quality of care was comparable in both countries while ease of navigation and payment was not. The inquiry then turned to sources and inputs, on the premise that a call to action needs to know who to talk to and which organisations to consult first. One participant asked what the actual causes are and listed five: political and legal ramifications, bureaucratic red tape, the commercialisation of healthcare throwing up barriers, a personnel and accreditation shortage with nurses leaving the field, and insurance friction that keeps practitioners out of it. Subject-matter experts at an insurer and clinicians in private practice were proposed as the people to ask, with the list to be folded into the Lyceum summary.
beats.pullQuote: What are the actual possible causes that would put us in this situation
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide: five candidate causes as numbered boxes (political and legal, red tape, commercialisation, personnel and accreditation, insurance friction), with a who-to-ask column naming insurers and private practice clinicians.

beats.title: Where a person starts looking
beats.summary: Asked where a family should actually look for reliable information rather than calling clinics at random, the circle named the provincial health authority a person belongs to as the structure that determines which services apply. The stronger answer was the general practitioner: the first person to go to, the knowledge base, the one with connections and the judgement about when and where to refer, with the relationship and a written list of questions doing most of the work. The same answer carried its own shortage, since general practice was described as less attractive than hospital-based practice. A nurse practitioner filling the role in one country was set against scope-of-practice rules in some American states that require a medical doctor to prescribe and to see patients, which concentrates demand on too few physicians and pushes routine cases into emergency departments meant for threats to life, limb and eyesight.
beats.pullQuote: For me myself. It all starts with the Gp.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide two: a referral ladder from general practitioner to specialist to hospital, with provincial health authorities as the enclosing box, and a side panel on scope of practice and the nurse practitioner question.

beats.title: Coverage as a moving target
beats.summary: Asked how insurance works inside the comparatively closed world of military healthcare, the circle set out how the plan runs: it permits out-of-network providers, which makes choosing a doctor easier, alongside ordinary copays and dental bought separately. Public programmes were described as convoluted: Medicare and Medicaid are widely confused for each other, the lettered parts have to be learned, and understanding any of it takes hours of unpaid self-directed research that most people do not have. A second account followed the same coverage forward in time: a lifetime entitlement that runs until an age at which Medicare becomes primary and the military plan becomes a supplement, monthly fees paid up front, copays, and tiers from basic to generous, generally better than what is commercially available but ending at a point that leaves whatever an employer or Medicare provides. Long-term and end-of-life care were named as costlier and more complex, with enrolment windows that have to be hit exactly. Commercial plans were described as caring less about taking care of people, and many in the United States were said to wish for the universal promise Canada makes, even acknowledging its shortage of primary care providers and staff.
beats.pullQuote: it's all convoluted like a lot of people don't know the difference between Medicare and Medicaid
beats.slideHint: Application slide on coverage over a lifetime: a timeline from enrolment through retirement to older age, showing where a military plan becomes a supplement and Medicare becomes primary, with fees, copays and enrolment windows marked and long-term care at the far end.

beats.title: No standard price
beats.summary: Two government-funded programmes run by separate organisations were described meeting at a single bedside, one picking up what the other does not cover, which puts bureaucracy at the point of care. Because the circle spanned ages, end-of-life questions were abstract for some and near for others, and education about universal healthcare was offered as the need rather than waiting for a threshold age to change everything at once. Access was said to vary by state, by city and by economic station. The concrete illustration was pricing: two hospitals across the street from one another quoted different prices for the same prescription, with hospitals effectively setting their own prices and no standardisation, so a patient who did not know to ask simply paid what the provider said. The same variation was reported for procedures, sometimes within a single hospital, so insurers are not the only cause of overpricing. A counter-argument held that a surgeon of thirty years and one newly qualified are not paid the same, so one price is not obvious; the reply was that patients are rarely told who will operate and should be offered the choice, and one participant reported having had the less experienced surgeon purely because that was the shortest wait. Disclosure of standard prices was offered as the common-sense mitigation, on the ground that information is what lets a person choose.
beats.pullQuote: there was no standardization of medicine.
beats.slideHint: Opportunities and Challenges slide on price: same prescription, two hospitals, two prices, with the gas station analogy as a visual and a standardisation-versus-experience balance beneath it.

beats.title: Care of last resort, and the game of surprise
beats.summary: One participant, from experience in law enforcement, raised the part of the system most citizens never see: people with no coverage sometimes reach care only by entering a public institution that is legally required to provide and pay for treatment, which absorbs a five-figure cost, has no way to recover it from someone without income, and writes it off. The point offered was that this is a small share of the population but a real route to care, and that nobody encounters it without professional contact. The insured contrast came from the same section: after a hospital delivery the bill arrives a week to a month later as an explanation of benefits with a five-figure share, so no informed choice about anaesthesia or an extra night in hospital is possible at the moment it would matter, standard stays being two days for a natural delivery and three for a caesarean. A $300 ambulance charge outside the plan made the same point smaller and sharper. Nobody, it was argued, can weigh a $1 apple against a $2 one when the price is disclosed only afterwards.
beats.pullQuote: it's almost like the game of surprise
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide on price opacity: a timeline showing service first and price weeks later, with an explanation of benefits mock-up, the ambulance charge as a small line item, and institutions of last resort noted as the fallback route to care.

beats.title: Take the insurance out
beats.summary: Opening opportunities and challenges formally, the facilitator set paying for experience against standardisation, and asked whether the United States should aspire to the universal systems already running in Canada and Japan or continue as it is. The strongest position of the evening answered that there should be no insurance and that care should not be commercialised at all, illustrated by a described contrast between a Canadian hospital's billing function of one person emailing government for payment and an American hospital's room full of people chasing payment. A more unusual proposal followed, attributed to England's National Health Service and offered without certainty that it is true: give everyone an annual notional pot, say $50,000, and let them watch it draw down, a doctor visit taking $275, so people gain a personal sense of what their care costs, with the pot topped up rather than anyone turned away for serious illness. The facilitator reframed it as an anonymised view of what people of a given age typically need; the reply held the simpler purpose, personal understanding of cost, with fewer emergency visits for minor illness as a side effect.
beats.pullQuote: There should be no insurance. It should not be commercialized.
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide: two billing departments side by side, one desk against a full room, beside a mock annual healthcare pot drawing down by visit, with 'universal care as an aspiration' as the header question.

beats.title: Triage by phone, and the case for the market
beats.summary: A provincial nurse line reachable by phone was named as a working intervention: a nurse gives guidance on whether a symptom warrants an emergency visit or can be managed at home. It exists partly because physicians are scarce and people without a doctor default to emergency departments, so the first answer, go see your doctor, is unavailable to many. A military nurse hotline was named as the same mechanism inside another system. Telehealth was proposed as the next step, with assessment over a phone camera and a prescription where that is all that is needed, saving time, staff and money, and with a library terminal offered as an access point for people without a camera of their own. Against the evening's drift, one participant then made the case that commercialisation buys standards: a large share of elective surgery, medical students sent from other countries to train, and malpractice exposure and insurance filtering out poor practitioners. Government-employed military doctors were offered as the contrast, with service members who prefer civilian providers, and out-of-network choices made for ease of scheduling.
beats.pullQuote: we have a lot of people don't have a doctor. So you go to emergency.
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide two: a triage funnel from nurse line and telehealth through primary care to emergency, with a facing panel listing the pros claimed for a commercial system - elective capacity, training destination, malpractice filtering.

beats.title: A call to action, and two volunteers
beats.summary: The facilitator closed the sequence by explaining what the call to action is for: so that collective wisdom is carried forward rather than left to disappear into the ether, with a storyboard produced for later gatherings. One participant volunteered to research the inquiry and start a document, without claiming to know where it would lead, and named the questions already in hand - how other countries administer care, including African countries, who funds Doctors Without Borders and where that money comes from, and what opportunities exist for people elsewhere. A second participant volunteered to partner on it as a topic worth learning more about. The host was to connect the two and open a shared document, so that a person arriving later with the same question starts from the circle's baseline rather than from nothing.
beats.pullQuote: They don't have to start with a blank slate.
beats.slideHint: Call to Action slide: the inquiry restated at the top, two volunteer slots filled, the open questions listed beneath (comparative national systems, African countries, Doctors Without Borders funding), and the shared document named as the mechanism.

beats.title: Reflection, fellowship, and the close
beats.summary: The learning reflection questionnaire went up for phones, and the session's running tech problem surfaced as a procedural finding: a participant dialling in by phone could reach neither the on-screen QR code nor the chat, so the link had to be offered by email as a fallback. It had also been posted in the chat, logged at chat clock 01:08:49, which is @1:04:04 on the recording. No deadline was attached to the survey, and answering it later was explicitly allowed. The fellowship circle then opened as a final round, with the reminder that silence itself is a contribution and that nobody need speak to complete their time. Thanks were given for patience through the tech issues, a first for the facilitator, to be noted for refining how the online Lyceum is delivered and eventually for holding these in person. One participant closed on the stake behind the question, that people do not go to hospital because they have no money for it, and welcomed participants back for future gatherings. A late arrival in the final minute apologised for coming in at the end and was asked to stay on after the close, and the recording ended at @1:09:22.
beats.pullQuote: There's people that don't go to the hospital just because they don't have money for it.
beats.slideHint: Learning Reflection slide with the post-survey QR code and a short link fallback for the chat, then the Fellowship Circle closing slide carrying the 'silence is a contribution' line and a placeholder for the next Lyceum.

inquiries.withheld: Material withheld under the archive's privacy rules: participants' names, relationships between participants, biographical and professional detail from the introductions round, family circumstances, immigration circumstances, health, personal finances, contact details, anything involving a minor, and the names of people who were not present and could not consent.

inquiries.inquiry: What should leaders do to empower education and communities?
inquiryAliases: What should leaders do to empower education in communities?

meeting.landAcknowledgement: No spoken land acknowledgement was given; the opening was a breathing exercise with gratitude prompts for the Earth, ancestors, self, family, and the next generation. One participant typed gratitude in the chat for living and learning on the stolen lands of the Squamish, Tsleil-Waututh and Musqueam Nations, and A participant added that they grew up in Ocean County, New Jersey learning about the Lenape. Canada's land acknowledgement practice and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission were later discussed as an example of a country teaching a fuller history.

The Department of Education was a back-office body with little influence on schools.
Left to their own devices, states might not do what serves America best.
Federal grants and priorities reinforced underserved communities at primary and secondary level.
Schools testing better on standardized tests receive more money, compounding the gap.
With no national curriculum, competing ideas of the nation leave no common identity.
Federal funding compensates underserved communities underfinanced by tax and property based systems.
Inequality once formed may take two or three generations to rebalance.
Desegregation of schools happened for the students but not for the teachers.
Programs a nation runs show what that country places most value on.
Part of an education can come from adults who are not technically educators.
A federal government withdrawing from provision leaves communities carrying it, housing then education.

Department of Defense schools on post - new smart boards and almost unlimited resources.
