Crowded email inboxes bury the message among competing demands for attention.
International communities have shifted from working together toward what they can get.
Growing this community requires vulnerability and love, which many find difficult.
Leaders who deal out division cards make divisions harder to look past.
Younger people, shaped by technology, lack practice starting unpolarized conversations.

inquiries.quote: It almost seems like it's a collective responsibility and a collective call to action.
inquiries.callToAction: The call to action stayed with the whole circle rather than one champion: each participant is asked to find a way to build the community in their own sphere of influence, from inviting someone to a Lyceum to watching for local events where the work can be introduced, and the facilitator will follow up by email. One participant volunteered to forward the recorded conference presentation to a rabbi, a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations. Another offered to share that same conference video with a university professor and with further contacts as ideas surface. A third plans to approach the Common Ground Scholar network of clergy to see who is willing to amplify the message in their own communities, will create social media content from this and earlier Lyceums through the summer, and will add and visualize connections to partner organizations on the website. A fourth will list past Lyceums there in digestible, searchable form with ways to volunteer. Shinrin-yoku flyers will be redrawn in bright hand-drawn nature art with the nature games named on them. A young participant suggested seeking permission to post nonprofit flyers at a school, and the circle put forward a Praxium podcast and short Lyceum clips as content to make next.

storyboard.logline: After an eight-month pause, a Praxium circle spread from Lima to Los Angeles gave an evening, and then some, to one question: how to grow the learning community.
storyboard.arcNotes: The session opened tightly scripted - norms, pre-survey, land gratitude, introductions - and stayed personal longer than usual because eight months of life had piled up: a retirement, an 80-hour coaching certification, a thesis nearing its end, a family living abroad in Lima. The discussion opened up twice. First when the questions were handed to the young participants at the table, whose answers - a school fundraiser run drawing two hundred people, posters cleared with the school, bright hand-drawn nature pictures, games named on the flyer - reframed outreach from adult marketing into something a child would pick up. Second when a participant asked why anyone should have to leave the country for cultural experience, which turned the room inward: Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, immigrants already arriving in America, one subway stop between worlds in the Bronx, an older neighbor's steps shoveled in Pittsburgh. Convergence came from a communications-theory frame offered late in the evening - person to person, then groups, then broad social media, run simultaneously with tailored messaging - which the participant who had opened the inward turn adopted explicitly at the close. The last third narrowed to obstacles that are practical rather than ideological: crowded inboxes, complaint without solutions, scarce attention. The call to action was left deliberately undelegated, owned by everyone in their own sphere of influence with follow-up by email, and the closing circle ran past time through vulnerability, similarities over wedges, heart rather than regulation, and the website roadmap.

beats.title: Reopening after eight months
beats.summary: The facilitator opened by welcoming the circle to the first Lyceum in about eight months, the last having been in November 2025, and read the structural norms for a shared purpose meeting - every person a peer, every voice welcome, safe and respectful comment, seek commonality while respecting difference - asking that the young guests present be encouraged to speak. The ninety-minute agenda was walked through, with the note that the question was pre-determined, so no time would go to deliberating what to discuss. A two-question pre-survey went up by QR code asking whether each person needed to be helped, hugged or heard and how the circle could help; answers were read aloud at one table, one participant observed that their own responses were no longer anonymous, and another offered a hug across the call.
beats.pullQuote: Hey man, if you need a hug, we can give you a hug, you know?
beats.slideHint: Title slide plus Rules and Structural Norms for 'June Lyceum - 28 June 2026', an agenda strip (pre-survey, present circle, shared understanding, sequence of inquiry, post-survey, closing circle), then the pre-survey QR code with a short link fallback for the chat and both questions spelled out.

beats.title: Present circle and land gratitude
beats.summary: The facilitator led the opening presence as a deliberate stop to the day's hustle, Monday's meetings and tomorrow's problems, orienting the circle toward place, family, self and children. Standing in for the usual Canadian land acknowledgement, the gratitude went to the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela rivers in Pennsylvania, with Monongahela translated as 'fallen banks' and each person invited to consider the heritage of their own ground. The facilitator then modeled the shared understanding round first: Army service, and three months in Europe in support of Ukraine since the last gathering, with home defined as the people one feels connected to rather than a fixed address.
beats.pullQuote: home is just people that I feel connected to
beats.slideHint: Opening / Present Circle slide: land acknowledgement text naming the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela watershed with the 'fallen banks' translation, and the three shared-understanding prompts (cultural background, where you call home, what has happened since the last Lyceum).

beats.title: Lima, young voices, and coaching
beats.summary: A participant joining from Lima, Peru introduced the group gathered there, where a two-day conference on spirituality and religion in society had just finished, and framed the stay as a chance to build community in Latin America. The young participants were then given space to introduce themselves in their own words, and one answered the cultural identity prompt by claiming many cultures and putting home wherever the family is. Another participant reported from Texas on completing an 80-hour executive, life and goal-setting coaching course they had first been skeptical of, valuing it for drawing out people's own realizations. The same voice named Parents in Action as the newest channel, focused on developing children for what is coming, and reported more allies and network than at the last Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: thank you ... for putting this on and creating the space for us to practice the Lyceum as this endeavor for shared purpose
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding slide: the three prompts small in the corner, a Lima photo strip for the conference on spirituality and religion in society, and a callout box for the two newer channels - coaching (80-hour certification) and Parents in Action.

beats.title: Retirement, service, and a thesis
beats.summary: One participant announced a retirement, recommended it to anyone working toward it, and described taking over maintenance at their synagogue on the grounds that the congregation has plenty of lawyers, doctors and judges but few people who can drive a nail straight. Another named retired Army life as the strongest thread in a mixed cultural background and said they are still trying to make sense of a lot of uncertainty. A third attendee, showing only as an unrecognized string of letters, was invited to come off mic: born in Belize and long settled in Los Angeles, entering the tail end of a thesis on Belizean women and mother-daughter bonding. Every introduction converged on the same answer to where home is.
beats.pullQuote: No matter where I am, my family is where home is.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding continued: round-robin list with one line for each person, the repeated answer 'home is where the family is' pulled out as a large callout, and a small footnote that a device name hid an attendee until they introduced themselves on mic.

beats.title: The map and the question
beats.summary: A colored world map placed the circle across the United States, Europe, the Caribbean and South America, used to make the point that what is a problem for one person may not be a problem for another. The facilitator walked the sequence of inquiry the evening would follow: theories and concepts, application, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, then a call to action. The topic was tied to the Praxium's first annual meeting at the beginning of June, called a milestone, and the single question for the night was set. The facilitator also noted a personal arc, from wondering two years ago what there was to add to now guiding this Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: how do we grow the Praxium learning community? How do we get more people involved?
beats.slideHint: Two slides: colored world map with attendee locations pinned and the Caribbean inset called out, then Today's Inquiry - 'How do we grow the Praxium learning community?' - with the sequence of inquiry listed down the side as the evening's roadmap.

beats.title: Lived experience and trusted conduits
beats.summary: One participant argued the message can grow because it is fundamentally about humanity, and that the group's lived experience carries further than theory does, reporting consistently warm reception with no substantive pushback, especially for coaching aimed at veterans moving into civilian communities. Another put the same question to the young participants at the table, asking where they had seen families and community members show up at school rather than only students. One of them named the Terry Fox run, a lap-based school fundraiser for cancer research drawing roughly two hundred people, which produced the night's first concrete channel: local events and schools. A further participant then described discussing the video of the Lima conference presentation with a rabbi that day and forwarding it that evening, treating the rabbi as a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations, while the facilitator pointed to the existing Facebook and LinkedIn work and short clips cut from Lyceums.
beats.pullQuote: We're tired of sitting in the passenger seat getting told, hey, this is where we're going. No, we want to get in the driver's seat and we want to lead.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: bullets for message rooted in humanity, lived experience over theory, reception to date, veteran transition coaching, and local events and schools as an untapped audience (Terry Fox run, about 200 attendees), with 'driver's seat, not passenger seat' as the banner line.

beats.title: Flyers a kid would read
beats.summary: A participant asked the young participants how to reach children about the Shinrin Yoku forest bathing offering, a six-month project whose flyers and email lists only reach adults. Their answers were specific: posters put up at school with permission, bright hand-drawn nature pictures instead of adult-oriented documents, and naming the nature games on the flyer so children know games are part of the immersion. The same participant noted that learners in their sixties and seventies already run alongside children at these events, and a further suggestion that the material include everyone led back to the mission language of fellowship through diversity. The facilitator added mediums beyond social media - a scoreboard advertisement at a Pirates game, radio, a Praxium podcast running interviews - and another participant asked permission to share the conference video with a university professor, which was granted without restriction.
beats.pullQuote: if you're talking about making hand-drawn images of things that kids would naturally want to see, you're right
beats.slideHint: Channels and Amplifiers slide: two columns, trusted conduits (clergy, professors, veteran networks, shared video) and mediums (Facebook, LinkedIn, shorts, podcast, radio, event advertising), plus a mock kid-facing Shinrin Yoku flyer - bright colors, hand-drawn nature, games named, multiple generations shown.

beats.title: Framing outward, building in Lima
beats.summary: The facilitator opened the application section on making a message land outside America, using Pittsburgh dialect ('yinz' where others say 'y'all') and World Cup visitors discovering ranch dressing as examples of how accidentally local a message can be. A participant described Alternative Peru, the nonprofit another member of the circle found, whose guided excursions deliberately skip the standard Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary. Young participants recounted a week of community building in Lima: homework help and play at a children's library, a dance hall mixing indigenous and Latin music, a meal in a local family's home where the hosts asked what the visitors made of Peru, and a boatyard where they met the local craftsman who builds most of the boats. The participant who had introduced Alternative Peru drew the summarizing point that these are the things residents actually do, and that curiosity and broken Spanish were enough to start the conversations.
beats.pullQuote: we've gone to a children's library to help out with, like, their homework, and we've been playing with them
beats.slideHint: Application slide: 'how is this handled around the world' with the Alternative Peru non-tourist model listed against the standard tourist itinerary, four Lima examples as icons (library, dance hall, shared meal, boatyard), and a caption on messaging that travels past its own dialect.

beats.title: Citizens of the world
beats.summary: The facilitator described meeting nonprofit organizations while in Europe that act as a central hub between donors and people in need, and using those conversations to introduce the Praxium's work with veterans and across generations. Asked how the family living abroad explains ending up in Peru, the participant joining from there said the answer given is that they are citizens of the world, learning and loving together by doing it physically rather than talking about it. That participant framed travel as resilience practice and suggested that a family who travels can role model the practice for families who have not considered it. Another participant and the facilitator both affirmed the shaping effect of such experience, the facilitator recalling helping build houses in Mexico and needing a translator to connect.
beats.pullQuote: I've been really telling people that we're citizens of the world, and that we're trying to learn and love together
beats.slideHint: Application continued: 'citizens of the world' as the header, with a three-step ladder (exposure, experience, resilience) and a side panel on nonprofits as donor-to-resource hubs and interconnecting older and younger generations.

beats.title: The next neighborhood over
beats.summary: Prompted by the land acknowledgement being brought home to Pennsylvania, one participant turned the inquiry inward and asked how to encourage people into a different neighborhood in their own city instead of a foreign country. The facilitator framed members as ambassadors for a better community and proposed using social media to show where each person is and how they are connected to the land they live on. Another participant described volunteering with Habitat for Humanity on the west side of Los Angeles and argued that immigrants already arriving in America should be made to feel welcome, because the communities needing help are right here. The facilitator matched that with shoveling snow and helping older neighbors without vehicles reach appointments through a hard Pittsburgh winter, and a third participant with Pelham Parkway in the Bronx, where one subway stop moved you between Jewish, Italian and Chinese neighborhoods.
beats.pullQuote: you really only had to go a subway stop down the way and you were in a different world
beats.slideHint: Application - Cultural exchange at home: reframe banner 'you do not have to leave the country to cross a culture', with three worked examples (Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, welcoming immigrants already here, a Bronx subway stop between neighborhoods) and a small prompt asking each attendee to name one neighborhood they have never visited.

beats.title: Three fronts at once
beats.summary: One participant supplied the evening's organizing frame from communications theory: person-to-person engagement as the building block, then groups and affinity groups, then the much broader community reachable through social media. Assessing the Praxium as working mostly person-to-person with some group and social media effect, the same voice argued the three have to run simultaneously, with messaging tailored to each audience while the core message holds. The facilitator connected that to holding public Lyceums in a commonplace room that needs no Teams link, computer, tablet or internet, where a person can walk in and be helped, heard or hugged. That closed the loop back to the pre-survey question of how each person arrives.
beats.pullQuote: But doing all three simultaneously is probably the most effective way to grow the effort overall.
beats.slideHint: Scaling model slide: three-tier diagram (individual, group and affinity, broad social media) with 'run all three at once, tailor the messaging, hold the core message' beneath, and a side note on in-person public Lyceums with no technology barrier tied back to helped / heard / hugged.

beats.title: Common ground and veterans
beats.summary: One participant recast the sources question as building the network and the team on top of several years of groundwork, and marketing the group's relevance and impact on communities. Another named the Common Ground Scholar collaborative, whose two-day conference drew over two hundred participants including Buddhist, Orthodox Christian, Muslim and Jewish clergy, as a network worth asking to amplify the message in their own communities. That same participant recounted a dinner conversation with a veteran who keeps military service off a professional profile but volunteered it once the Praxium's message came up, and the W. E. B. Du Bois challenge, written from Ghana, to veterans who fought for democracy abroad; the takeaway offered was the common ground network plus veterans groups, with service out of uniform as the framing. A third participant said the conversation kept generating more places to share the video, the facilitator pointed to existing small groups such as a Saturday running group as ready-made openings, and a fourth called a group run forest bathing on the road.
beats.pullQuote: you fought for liberty abroad, but why can't you do it at home?
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide: who and what is needed - Common Ground Scholar and interfaith clergy, veteran service organizations, the Kintsugi campaign, existing affinity groups such as running and fellowship groups - with the Du Bois challenge as the pull quote and 'service, just not in uniform' as the framing line.

beats.title: Complaint, universality, and saying hello
beats.summary: The facilitator described the military family skill of getting a household linked into a community, a religious group or some fellowship on arrival so nobody sits staring at four walls, and noted how much the younger generation struggles to build that kind of connection, then named a habit seen in military culture and beyond - complaining without solutions - and proposed answering it by asking people how they would actually fix the problem if handed authority for a day, with community as the honest answer. One participant held that the human experience is universal wherever you go, the same fear, joy, need for belonging and wanting the best for your family, and only the difficulty varies; that participant described greeting strangers in the street in a country of birth, missing that for years, and now saying hello first even when nobody answers, because their own part has been done. Another added that a first hello can open an entire dialogue, and that whatever problem someone is stuck on, somebody out there has already lived it and holds wisdom worth asking for.
beats.pullQuote: most of the time it's more of just complaining without solutions
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide split in two: on the left the pattern to break (complaint without solutions, four walls on arrival, younger generation out of practice), on the right the low-cost moves (say hello first, ask how they would fix it, assume someone has already solved it), under the header 'the human experience is universal'.

beats.title: Inbox noise and priorities
beats.summary: The facilitator turned to opportunities and challenges and named communicating meaningfully with people who are all in a hurry as the hardest of them. One participant sharpened it to inboxes full of people demanding attention and competing for time and resources, and asked how anything rises above that noise. In reply, the facilitator said no magical filter exists, and that three months away from a phone had shown how few things actually matter, retelling a lecture demonstration in which golf balls stand for the few big priorities, gravel and sand for everything that fills the gaps, and a poured beer for the room left to have fun. The practice described was writing down a top three and slowing down deliberately - forest bathing, a walk with a podcast, a quiet cup of coffee - and another participant said writing things down and forest bathing both work for them.
beats.pullQuote: how do you separate the wheat from the chaff
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide: bullets for attention scarcity, inbox noise, busy schedules and the difficulty of being heard, paired with a jar graphic (golf balls, gravel, sand, beer) and the practices column - top three written down, mindfulness, time in nature.

beats.title: A collective call to action
beats.summary: Rather than naming one champion for the topic, the facilitator made the call to action collective and said it would come as a follow-up email: each person decides how they will contribute to building the community in their own sphere of influence. The offers already on the table were named - sharing the conference video, inviting people to a Lyceum, reaching out locally, posting to social media - with a challenge to everyone to make the difference where they are. One participant answered simply that they would do it. Another adopted the three fronts named earlier in the evening explicitly for the summer, noted that families off school spend more time on social media, and committed to creating Lyceum content for the Facebook and LinkedIn presence heading into fall.
beats.pullQuote: it almost seems like it's a collective responsibility and a collective call to action
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead / Call to Action slide: 'In what way can you contribute to building this community?' with the four offers already on the table listed beneath, the follow-up email named as the mechanism, and a summer-into-fall timeline strip for the social media content.

beats.title: Reflection survey and gratitude
beats.summary: The learning reflection questionnaire went out as the last slide, answered anonymously and explicitly not used to track anyone down, with the link dropped into chat for whoever could not scan it. Opening the final round, the facilitator thanked the circle for the chance to guide the evening after eight months apart, and noted who was joining from where, including a family in Peru and a colleague coming off a field rotation. Recalling work with international communities that had drifted from what they could build together toward what they could get out of it, the facilitator described telling them to imagine instead what they could all do together, credited the Lyceum's mix of places and experiences for both its camaraderie and its reach, then joked about sour Pittsburgh first impressions and the steel companies that left.
beats.pullQuote: if you could do this by yourself, like, imagine what we could all do together
beats.slideHint: Post-Survey slide: learning reflection QR code with the chat-link fallback, the two prompts (what spoke to you today, what should the next Lyceum take up), a note that answers are anonymous, and a closing-round marker underneath.

beats.title: Vulnerability and shared similarities
beats.summary: One participant named pride and the human wish to be seen as good enough as the material the circle is working with, and said the hard part is holding love and vulnerability alongside the work of meeting people where they are; asked to repeat it, that participant said it again. Still working through the questionnaire on a shifted screen, the same voice asked forgiveness for being a little technically challenged, then, invited to give closing remarks, picked up the Bronx story told earlier by another participant: two blocks over in New York City is another world, so you do not have to travel around the world to see the world, and much of the change the group wants can happen inside America. A further participant agreed and argued that focusing on similarities and mutual help, rather than driving wedges, is what keeps a collective from breaking into smaller groups that argue and bicker.
beats.pullQuote: you don't have to travel around the world to actually see the world
beats.slideHint: Closing Circle slide one: two facing panels - 'be vulnerable, meet people where they are' and 'similarities over wedges' - with the restated reframe across the bottom, that seeing the world can start two blocks away.

beats.title: Heart, and the website roadmap
beats.summary: The facilitator observed that when the person in charge is the one handing out division cards, looking past the divisions gets harder, and one participant answered that a community should not need laws and regulations to behave decently; the facilitator named heart for service as the thing underneath. That same participant also said they had been reserved but feel more and more comfortable in their share each time they come back, and the circle said it was glad to have that experience and those studies on the calls. Another participant called the group's real contribution the creation of space for dialogue, where people who sit at different points on the political spectrum can air differences without cutting each other's throats, and the facilitator added that technology has cost some of the younger generation the mannerisms for starting such a conversation. The closing remarks came back to the Praxium's calls to action through the Kintsugi campaign, the Lyceum and social media; one participant added the website work on visualizing connections to partner organizations and another the plan to list previous Lyceums in a digestible, searchable form with ways for people to volunteer, before thanks and goodnights slightly over time.
beats.pullQuote: We shouldn't need laws and regulations.
beats.slideHint: Final slide pair: the Praxium offerings as calls to action (Lyceum, Kintsugi, Shinrin Yoku, social media), then the website roadmap - partner organization map, searchable archive of previous Lyceums, volunteer sign-up - with a goodnight line and the next Lyceum placeholder.

inquiries.inquiry: How can an individual challenge an institution through the judicial process?

meeting.landAcknowledgement: Given for a Canadian-founded organization: gratitude to the native nations of the founding area in Canada, then extended to the communities and the ground each participant actually lives on, since the circle is now spread across coasts. Thanks were offered to self first, for showing up to be helped or heard, then to the families who support or take part in the work, then to the children the work is for, so that they can be good citizens, carry on traditions and stay involved in their communities.

Pre-survey by QR code, about two minutes to complete.
Opening and presence, with gratitude for the land, for family, and for children.

United Nations and color-coded World Bank maps, for cultural context beyond borders.

Sequence of Inquiry: theories, applications, sources and inputs, opportunities, challenges, way ahead.
Post-survey reflection questionnaire, each person raising a hand when finished.
Closing fellowship circle, foundation updates, and a farewell slide.
surveyPre: A quick survey by QR code on how each person is feeling.
Exact wording not recoverable: the questions were on screen and never read aloud.
surveyPost: A closing reflection questionnaire, completed before the fellowship circle.
Exact wording not recoverable: the questions were on screen and never read aloud.
contextNotes: Announced at the open: the Lyceum becomes monthly, on the first Sunday, at a standing time.
Scheduled for about ninety minutes; the circle closed about two minutes over.
Recording runs 1:38:34, with roughly fourteen minutes of arrival talk before the formal open.
Held online across coasts and time zones, the facilitator sharing slides throughout.

No topic was pre-determined; the question came from the floor when the facilitator invited one.
The question came from participants living the problem, and is generalized in this record.

That participant flagged the account as personal assessment shaped by frustration, not objective analysis.

theories.text: An ordinary person does not have the resources to fight the federal government.
The frame is challenging government through a judicial system, not two businesses competing.
Administrative bodies once offered an even playing ground for challenging the federal government.
That level playing field has changed significantly in the last year and a half.
Part of the change is replacing the judges who sit on these deciding bodies.
Anti-discrimination enforcement is recast as unconstitutional and as violating employer rights.
Hiring one's own attorney is the traditional route, and expensive for a recognized specialist.
Every person has a right to be heard and to address grievances with government.
Government should know that the citizenry will not roll over in silence.
A pro se precedent: law studied in jail, self-representation on appeal, and a win.
That precedent depended on having nothing but time to learn the process.
The claim: the system is designed not to support accountability when government is challenged.
Where legal routes narrow, drawing public attention becomes the remaining lever.
A grievance needs a shaped, effective form; complaining alone is not effective.
Grievances gain force when carried collectively; an individual alone is structurally outmatched.
Rules can change while a grievance is in progress; the forum entered is not the forum that decides.
A right costing more than a household holds is a right in name only.
The forum's fairness rested on informal norms, courtesy and respect for precedent, as much as on statute.
Matching a grievance to a body's existing constituency opens channels a general complaint cannot.

applications.text: One statute, different procedures for federal, private, municipal and state government employers.
Pro se filing - a non-attorney may run their own litigation, and always could.
A prisoner learned criminal law inside, appealed pro se in district court, and won.
The ACLU - two mothers pooled resources to challenge police violence across court systems.
Reimagining Safety - documentary comparing policing in Canada and the United States.
For Our Children - mothers who lost children to police brutality banded together.
Constituent services - junior staffers read inquiries and raise significant ones up the office.
A legislator's committee seat decides fit: Armed Services for a service-linked grievance.
Veterans groups went to Capitol Hill together against proposed disability cuts.
Revolutionary War era - citizens pressed the government to pay for land it used.
Immigration and customs processes - little progress without an attorney to submit evidence.

sources.text: Pro bono firms and public interest nonprofits that contest change in the EEO system.
A recognized firm, or a good attorney anywhere, willing to fight cases in the current system.
Attorneys able to work on a reduced fee or contingency basis.
Nonprofits willing to donate toward a crowdfunding effort for legal costs.
Senators Tim Kaine and Mark Warner of Virginia; Kaine sits on the Armed Services Committee.
Knowledge of constituent services: junior staffers read inquiries and raise them up the chain.
Military OneSource as a source of links to organizations that represent veterans.
Veterans groups such as the VFW and Disabled American Veterans, for litigator referrals.
Two documentaries offered for the circle to watch: Reimagining Safety, and For Our Children.
Historical case law, precedents and past citizen-versus-government battles, asked of the group.
Pro se filing needs training in the systems, tactics and procedures, not just will.
Multiple channels contacted at once, since any single one may never respond.
More participants in the circle, so more expertise is on hand for problems.
Volunteers, memberships, and library contributions of stories, resources and technical knowledge.
Representation whose availability does not depend on what a household can pay.
A plain map of the complaint route, which no claimant assembles without an insider.
A written account of the process learned here, so a later inquiry does not restart it.

policies.text: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission - administrative judges, then the Commission itself, decide claims against federal agencies.
Federal statute lets any civilian employee lodge an EEOC complaint against their own agency.
The responding agency investigates internally first; its final decision can then be appealed to the Commission.
Merit Systems Protection Board and National Labor Relations Board cases run the same administrative route.
Appeal to a federal district court judge is the administrative system's ultimate pressure valve.
Executive orders used as the instrument for changing what the law requires.
Supreme Court rulings let the president remove appointees from statutorily independent bodies.
Prior EEOC enforcement now called woke, unconstitutional, and a violation of employers' rights.
A proposed EEOC regulation would deny individual claimants a hearing before the Commission.
Administrative judges given new criteria: a very high threshold to find government discrimination.
American Bar Association - whether its certification is required to file motions was questioned.
The statute did not change; enforcement posture, procedure and personnel did.

opportunities.text: A standing monthly slot, first Sunday, lets invitees plan attendance in advance.
Saybrook University classes as a route to more Lyceums, after one ran as a class project.
Website inquiries reach every member, since no filtering has been set up.
Documentary attention could pull judicial, legislative, or financial support toward a stalled case.
Senators Tim Kaine and Mark Warner named as channels; Kaine sits on Armed Services.
Friends and family can petition a representative on someone's behalf, not only the aggrieved.
A shaped, actionable request gets traction where an unfocused complaint does not.
A message carried by others affected can land harder than a first-person account.
Whistleblower protections suggest a model for shielding people who raise grievances.
Two members volunteered to help craft the message and to send it themselves.
An offer to ask around for attorneys known to be effective with outcomes.
Running several channels at once raises the chance that one of them answers.
A storyboard carried to the next gathering keeps a live problem under review.
Pro bono executive and life coaching hours offered to members through Praxium.
Monthly cadence lets an unresolved inquiry be tracked forward rather than retold from scratch.

challenges.text: A private citizen cannot outspend a government with unlimited resources.
An institution can stall for time until the individual stops pursuing the case.
Past enforcement is now called woke and a violation of employers' rights.
A case with a fair chance eighteen months ago is now stifled at every level.
Emergency appeals reach enough appointee judges to halt the anti-discrimination process.
Adjudicators now demand near-absolute proof: video, pictures, a newspaper headline.
The Supreme Court, the final safeguard, is no longer a comfortable destination.
These cases no longer pay enough to attract attorneys willing to fight them.
Public interest and pro bono organizations are squeezed as donations dry up.
Legal nonprofits weigh volunteer time and choose policy fights over individual cases.
An appeal inside the commission can return to the judge who already ruled.
Asked how ordinary people manage, counsel offered only that some have will and means.
Civil liberties organizations may take eight weeks to answer a request, or never answer.
Constituent inquiries are read first by junior staffers, who decide what rises.
Sourcing claimant counsel through a government-side practitioner means approaching the opposing camp.
Self-representation is always available and rarely succeeds without training in the procedures.
No estimate of success is available, so choosing between routes is judgement rather than calculation.
The hour turned on one practitioner voice being present; without it, conversation without a way ahead.

inquiries.quote: Oh my gosh, how can I fight these folks? They've got unlimited resources.
inquiries.callToAction: The circle put three routes in front of the participants who brought the question - pro bono or nonprofit legal help, an elected representative, and public attention through film - and then narrowed the way ahead to one product: a written, actionable request to a representative, framed as a specific ask rather than a complaint, on the principle that complaining feels good but is not effective and that the recipient has to be helped to help. Two participants were asked to help craft that message and to send it under their own hand, pressing for a response; one of them had already offered to shape a real question and take it to a senator's office, and the circle agreed to meet separately from the Lyceum to write it. Whether the letter should speak as one household or as a wider grievance was left open. The named recipients were the offices of Senator Tim Kaine and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, one of them sitting on the Armed Services Committee; asking a senator's office for a referral was confirmed as an appropriate request, to be routed through constituent services, read by junior staff and raised up the chain only if it matches what the member is working on, so it must arrive as a concrete, doable ask. One participant undertook to inquire about attorneys known to be effective and consistently professional, while naming the constraint that doing so means reaching out to the opposing camp. The participants who brought the question keep the decision on which route to file and by when; both the routes and the date are withheld from this record. Left with the whole circle rather than one owner: watching the two documentaries raised in the discussion, Reimagining Safety and a second film whose title was given as 'for our children', and approaching veteran advocacy groups, the VFW and Disabled American Veterans among them, for a litigator who would look at a case of this kind. A request to the American Civil Liberties Union had already gone in before the gathering, with up to eight weeks for an answer and no guarantee of one. The facilitator undertook to stay in contact and to build a storyboard, so the next monthly Lyceum can open with an update and the inquiry can be carried rather than closed. Foundation business ran alongside: pro bono coaching sessions offered to any member who asks, continued education curriculum development, and further work on the website and its map of connections and partnerships.

storyboard.logline: A circle of seven across Canada and three United States time zones set itself a standing monthly rhythm, then gave its first session under that rhythm to a question one participant brought in live rather than prepared: how can an individual challenge an institution through the judicial process?
storyboard.arcNotes: The session had two halves and a hinge. The first half was procedural and warm: a standing monthly slot agreed, norms read short because everyone present was a returner, and the shared understanding round rewritten as an update round since the circle already knew one another. Two contributions from that round were worth keeping - a comparison of two immigrant histories that turned out to run the same course, and an argument for planting what one will not live to harvest. The hinge was the facilitator opening the floor before proposing a topic, and a participant answering with something live rather than something interesting. From there the evening changed character. A second participant generalised it at once - an ordinary person cannot outspend the federal government - and a third refined the wording until the question was about the judicial process rather than about money, which is the form the archive keeps. The long middle was expert testimony from a participant with federal EEO practice experience, and it was pessimistic: the administrative bodies that once let individuals hold the government to worker protection statutes have been recomposed, the appeal routes above them are unreliable, and the nonprofits that used to absorb such cases are triaging toward policy work. That testimony was offered explicitly as personal assessment, with the speaker naming their own cynicism and apologising for what it might cost in objectivity, and it was not accepted as a conclusion: another participant agreed with the legal logistics and argued that the point of being heard survives losing. Convergence, when it came, was not about which route to take but about form - shape an actionable request rather than a complaint, and know that a junior staffer reads it first. The evening ended with a call to action left as a working session rather than a delegation, and with the practical case for the new cadence: an unfinished matter can be carried forward next month instead of retold.

beats.title: Before the session: consent, inquiries, and a Lyceum in a classroom
beats.summary: Recording was handled deliberately before anything else: the host confirmed transcription had been switched on and a second device's recording was turned off so only one capture ran. Website inquiries were noted to reach every member, because no filtering had been set up to route them to one person. One participant reported having already run a Lyceum as a graduate class final project, using the format while the class chose its own subject - how to empower women in leadership positions - with about ten classmates taking part. The plan described was to take that storyboard to other professors at Saybrook, and to a university partnership office, as evidence the format travels outside the foundation.
beats.pullQuote: Would you all be interested to try it in your class as a way to start sharing the message
beats.slideHint: No slide yet - screen share had not been granted. A retrospective card would show the Lyceum format carried into a university classroom: the class storyboard, the topic the students chose, the count of classmates who joined, and the pitch to other faculty.

beats.title: Waiting for the circle
beats.summary: Arrivals ran past the half hour and the interval went to informal catch-up rather than the agenda. The circle assembled across Canada and three United States time zones, and one participant joined late after a long flight and some trouble getting a computer set up. Nothing from this stretch enters the record: the talk was family news, travel, summer plans and a long story about a ballgame, all of it household detail. The host used the time to settle on a start point and to request screen share.
beats.slideHint: No slide. The template title card waits while the host asks to share the deck.

beats.title: A standing monthly Lyceum, norms, and the pre-survey
beats.summary: The session opened with a change of rhythm. The Lyceum becomes a standing monthly gathering on roughly the first Sunday of each month at 6:30 Eastern, 5:30 Central and 3:30 Pacific, so members can block the time in advance and an invitation can name a fixed date rather than negotiate one. Norms were kept short because everyone present had attended before: mute when not speaking, and respect as the bottom line. The agenda was walked through - pre-survey, opening and presence, shared understanding, the inquiry, post-survey reflection, closing fellowship circle - and a QR-code survey went up with about two minutes to answer it. The opening presence turned to place: the organisation is Canadian and gratitude was given to the native nations of its founding area, extended to the communities and ground the participants actually live on, then to self, to family, and to the children the work is meant to serve.
beats.pullQuote: treat everybody with respect is the bottom line
beats.slideHint: Title card for the August Lyceum, then Rules and Norms, the agenda strip, the pre-survey QR code with the two questions, and the land acknowledgement slide.

beats.title: Shared understanding, reframed as updates
beats.summary: With the circle already familiar with one another, the usual prompts on cultural background and where you call home were set aside and one prompt was added in their place: what has happened since the last Lyceum. The round was framed as camaraderie rather than introduction. Two things from it belong in the archive. A level-one coaching certification through the International Coaching Federation was one session from complete, with pro bono practice intended before any paid work. And a trend was noted of middle schools teaching business and economics alongside public speaking, leadership and dealing with people, so that young people meet the marketplace before they leave school. A participant delayed by travel and equipment trouble was welcomed into the round while it was in progress.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding slide with the three standard prompts, the first two struck through and 'what has happened since the last Lyceum' written in at the bottom.

beats.title: Two offerings from the round
beats.summary: Two contributions from the update round carried past the personal. The first came out of a national convention in Washington DC held by the Filipino American National Historical Society, whose chapters gather every two years: across sessions and conversations, the arc of Filipino immigration into the United States and of Jewish immigration from Eastern Europe looked remarkably alike - different languages, different prejudices, and when watered down, far more in common than not. The second was an argument about time. Planting seedlings that will not bear fruit within one's own lifetime was offered as an act of faith, on the grounds that the trees a person sits under were planted by grandparents. The circle took it as a frame for work whose results nobody present will see.
beats.pullQuote: I sit under trees that my grandparents grew
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding continued, two panels: the DC convention beside the two immigration stories being compared, and a seedling standing for work whose harvest belongs to a later generation.

beats.title: Maps, then the floor
beats.summary: Two maps carried the standing cultural frame: the United Nations political map, noted as accurate only until borders change, and the colour-coded World Bank map, used to make the point that culture crosses borders through migration rather than stopping at them. The facilitator then opened the floor before proposing a topic, inviting any problem currently weighing on anyone. A participant answered with a matter their household is living through now, described as real and tangible rather than hypothetical, and offered it not as a request for sympathy but as raw material the circle could work with. The matter itself is withheld from this record. The question drawn out of it is not.
beats.pullQuote: that's something that's very real and tangible
beats.slideHint: The UN world map, then the colour-coded World Bank map, then the blank Inquiry slide that the host types into live.

beats.title: Shaping the question
beats.summary: A second participant stepped back from the particulars to state the general problem: an ordinary person does not have the resources to fight the federal government, and while right is right, a roof and a full refrigerator come first. The facilitator added the tactic that makes resources decisive - an adversary with effectively unlimited means can neglect a matter and stall for time until the individual no longer wants to pursue it - and drafted a first wording about the processes and procedures for an individual against a larger corporation or government entity. A participant then refined it away from economics: this is not two businesses competing and not private versus public sector, it is an attempt to walk into a system where one side holds a blank cheque. The wording the circle settled on asks how an individual can challenge an institution through the judicial process.
beats.pullQuote: how can I fight these folks? They've got unlimited resources.
beats.slideHint: The Inquiry slide mid-edit: the first draft about individual versus corporation or government entity struck through, and the final wording about challenging an institution through the judicial process typed underneath.

beats.title: Theories: a playing field that changed
beats.summary: A participant with federal EEO practice experience gave the concepts section, describing what used to be an even playing ground - the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the other administrative bodies through which an individual could hold the federal government to the laws Congress passed to protect workers. That ground was described as having shifted significantly within about eighteen months, by executive orders attempting to change what the law is, and by changes to who sits on the bodies that decide cases, turning them into social justice battlefields where there had been a mix of backgrounds, professional courtesy and respect for past decisions. Supreme Court rulings permitting removals from bodies the statutes made independent and partisan-balanced were named as the mechanism. The Commission's composition was described as gutted and its traditional enforcement abandoned as woke and as a violation of employers' rights against their employees, with emergency appeals reliably finding judges willing to halt anti-discrimination process, and a Supreme Court inclined to hold that federal employees should do what the president tells them.
beats.pullQuote: The little people were getting crushed left and right
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts: a ladder of the challenge route - agency, commission, district court, appeals court, Supreme Court - each rung annotated with what has changed at it in the last year and a half.

beats.title: What is left to play with, and a stated bias
beats.summary: Asked what an individual can actually do, the same participant separated the field from the moves available on it. Paying for one's own counsel works, but the practitioners who are recognised and still willing to fight these cases are scarce, because the system no longer pays off and no probability analysis can tell a claimant whether a case is a winner. Pro bono firms and public interest nonprofits remain, but donations are drying up and those organisations are analysing the battlefield and choosing policy fights over individual ones. At the administrative level a proposed regulation change would stop individual claimants from seeking a hearing at all, and administrative judges have been given a threshold so high that only video, photographs and a newspaper headline would meet it. The participant then qualified the entire assessment as personal, naming the bias, cynicism and disillusionment audible in it, and apologised for whatever that cost in objectivity - which the circle accepted as honesty rather than as a disqualification.
beats.pullQuote: I always used to be a big believer in the rule of law. And I'm becoming very cynical about it.
beats.slideHint: Theories continued as an options board: own counsel, pro bono firm, public interest nonprofit - each with cost, availability and current outlook, footed by a note that this is one practitioner's personal assessment.

beats.title: The right to be heard
beats.summary: The facilitator set the problem in a longer line, from private citizens seeking payment for land the government used during the Revolutionary War through the states-versus-federal disputes that followed, arguing that this fight is not new. A participant agreed with every point of the legal assessment and then declined its conclusion: the right of a person to be heard and to address grievances with their government is a cornerstone of the nation, so a case presented and lost is still a case heard, and a government should know that the citizenry will not roll over on the assumption that people stay silent. The advice was not to shoulder such a fight alone but to find someone willing to take it on pro bono as a fight against tyranny. The facilitator pressed the harder version of the question: what did the founders intend for people without resources, how did individuals file grievances before there was a bar association, and can a citizen stand up in court and say plainly that they have no representation. The same pattern was noted in federal immigration and customs processes, where red tape effectively requires an attorney before evidence can even be put forward.
beats.pullQuote: If you don't have resources, you can't fight a legal battle.
beats.slideHint: Theories continued: the right to petition government set against the cost of exercising it, with a short timeline of citizen-versus-government disputes running from the Revolutionary War forward.

beats.title: Applications: precedent, film, and a lawyer's answer
beats.summary: The applications section produced three routes. First, a self-representation precedent raised from a recently finished course: a man imprisoned who studied law inside, argued his own appeal and won, offered as proof the thing is possible for someone with nothing but time to spend on it. The name and the particulars of that case are withheld here and need verifying against a source more reliable than this recording. Second, documentary film as a route to social impact, drawn from a class on exactly that: Reimagining Safety, which sets policing in Canada against policing in the United States and asks what a safer society would look like, and a second film following Black American mothers whose sons were killed or permanently harmed by police, who banded together, pooled resources with the American Civil Liberties Union and pressed the systemic problem through several court systems. That suggested the ACLU itself as a body to approach; it had already been asked, with a reply promised in up to eight weeks and no guarantee of one at all. Third, publicity and fundraising - a donation campaign, or a story picked up by someone who would make a film of it and pull judicial, legislative or financial weight behind it. Against all three sat the answer a lawyer had already given when asked how ordinary people manage this at all.
beats.pullQuote: How do other people do this? And she said, Well, some people just have the will and the means
beats.slideHint: Applications: three cards - self-representation, documentary and media attention, civil liberties litigation - with the film named on the middle card and the eight-week wait noted on the third.

beats.title: Sources and inputs: who can be asked
beats.summary: The sources section turned to public office. Bills introduced without enough support die quietly, but a sitting representative or senator can be approached on a constituent's behalf, on the principle that they work for the people who elect them. A precedent was offered from officer candidate school, where clearance backlogs of six months or more - and in one case nearly a year past a commissioning date - left candidates waiting, and congressional inquiries were the lever people actually pulled. Three routes were counted on the board: a civil liberties organisation, legislative representatives, and a documentary or film. It was added that the affected person need not be the one who writes, since friends and family can approach their own representatives on someone's behalf, and that several channels run in parallel beat waiting on any single one to answer.
beats.pullQuote: at the end of the day they work for us
beats.slideHint: Source and Input: a fan-out from one individual to civil liberties organisations, congressional offices, veteran groups and documentary makers, with a note that the channels are run at once rather than in sequence.

beats.title: How to ask so the ask can be answered
beats.summary: The evening's strongest convergence was about form rather than route. A participant warned that an approach to any office cannot be a complaint - not that I was treated poorly and I want help, which feels good and does nothing - but must carry a shaped question and a specific request, because an official who is willing to help still has to be given something to act on. The participant with EEO practice experience confirmed the mechanism from the other side: such letters arrive constantly, are read by junior staff under the constituent services process, and move up the chain only when they are actionable and match what the member already cares about, and nine times out of ten it is a staffer rather than the member who makes the calls. The facilitator translated it into military habit - bring the problem, then a decision point and options, one two three - and proposed packaging a letter that states the situation, the reasons, the help needed and one concise request. One question was left open: whether the affected person, or someone speaking on their behalf, makes the more effective messenger.
beats.pullQuote: you just have to help him help you
beats.slideHint: Opportunities: a letter skeleton on the slide - situation, reasons, specific request, decision points - beside the constituent services path from inbox to junior staffer to member.

beats.title: Advocacy routes, and what self-representation really means
beats.summary: Veteran advocacy organisations were raised as a route with proven collective muscle, having recently mobilised on the Hill against proposed disability cuts; groups such as the Veterans of Foreign Wars and Disabled American Veterans might refer a litigator, and Military OneSource was named as a place to start gathering links. The circle also asked whether whistleblower protections could be mirrored for someone bringing an ordinary grievance, so that pursuing one would not mean putting life savings or a mortgage up as collateral. On self-representation the answer was blunt: filing pro se has always been available and rarely succeeds, because knowing a right exists is not the same as being trained in the systems, tactics, techniques and procedures for exercising it, or in operating as part of an organised group - the comparison drawn was a citizen climbing into an attack helicopter to meet an armoured advance. The procedural ladder was then laid out in general terms: an internal agency EEO investigation and final decision, appeal into the Commission process where administrative judges decide, and civil litigation in federal court after that, with the same structure applying across federal agencies and different rules for private, municipal and state employers. An aside acknowledged that outcomes can turn on how well an attorney knows the judge rather than how well they know the law.
beats.pullQuote: all they are is a pro se individual jumping in a helicopter.
beats.slideHint: Challenges: the self-representation helicopter analogy as the image, beside the procedural ladder from internal agency investigation to commission hearing to federal civil litigation.

beats.title: Way ahead, reflection, and the closing circle
beats.summary: The way ahead was deliberately left open rather than resolved. The matter stays on the board: it is to be storyboarded so the next monthly Lyceum can carry an update, which is the practical argument for the new cadence - an ongoing call to action can be tracked instead of restarted. The named action was a separate working session with the two participants who hold the legal and legislative experience, to craft the message and the specific ask. The post-survey reflection was answered privately, with raised hands signalling completion so the facilitator knew when to move on. The closing circle drew the general lesson: a larger circle means more expertise available to whoever brings the next problem, and it was the technical knowledge in the room that evening which turned a good conversation into a way forward. Thanks were given for holding space for a problem that was personal rather than philosophical, and for treating something a family is still enduring as work the group could take up.
beats.pullQuote: having a space like the Lyceum where we can bring this as a problem
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead and Call to Action with owners left as roles rather than names, then the post-survey reflection questions, then the Closing and Fellowship Circle slide.

beats.title: Foundation updates and farewell
beats.summary: The last stretch went to the organisation. Forest therapy and the Kintsugi campaign continue, and a curriculum development role has been filled, with work under way on programmes of instruction and on material for homeschooling families and parents, on the reasoning that no manual for parenting exists. Pro bono coaching hours were offered to the circle - executive or life coaching, at level one certification with accreditation to follow - the intention being to give at no cost, or for a small donation, what the corporate market charges heavily for, and it was noted that a coach supplies the process rather than expertise in the client's field, driving the way ahead through the person's own thinking. Volunteering, membership and contributions of stories, resources and technical knowledge to the library were named as ways in. The website is live, with a world map beginning to show where the Lyceum's reach and partnerships run. The session closed two minutes over time, with thanks for the unglamorous work that keeps it running.
beats.pullQuote: it's all the small muscle movements that still make a lot of this work
beats.slideHint: Who We Are and ways to engage: current projects (forest therapy, Kintsugi, curriculum development), the pro bono coaching offer, volunteer and membership routes, the website world map, then the farewell card.

inquiries.withheld: Material withheld under the archive's privacy rules: participants' names, relationships between participants, biographical and professional detail from the introductions round, family circumstances, immigration circumstances, health, personal finances, contact details, anything involving a minor, and the names of people who were not present and could not consent.
